explanation: Goodpasture syndrome is caused by antibodies directed against type IV collagen in the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes. Patients classically develop rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with hematuria and pulmonary hemorrhage.

wrongOptions.explanation: IgA nephropathy is associated with mesangial IgA deposition and recurrent hematuria occurring shortly after upper respiratory infections
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: URI + hematuria + mesangial IgA = IgA nephropathy

wrongOptions.explanation: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis occurs after streptococcal infection and is characterized by low complement levels and subepithelial hump-shaped deposits.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Recent strep infection + low C3 + subepithelial humps = PSGN

wrongOptions.explanation: Membranous nephropathy is a nephrotic syndrome associated with subepithelial immune complex deposition producing a spike-and-dome appearance.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Nephrotic syndrome + spike-and-dome deposits = Membranous nephropathy

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Hemoptysis + RPGN + linear IgG = Goodpasture syndrome

stem: A patient develops hematuria, renal biopsy demonstrates crescent formation with minimal immune complex deposition, and serology is positive for c-ANCA. Which of the following diseases is most strongly associated with this presentation?
explanation: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotizing vasculitis associated with positive c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA) antibodies. Patients commonly develop rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis with little or no immune complex deposition on immunofluorescence, producing a pauci-immune pattern.

wrongOptions.explanation: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immune complex–mediated nephritic syndrome associated with low complement levels and subepithelial hump-shaped deposits after streptococcal infection.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Recent strep infection + low C3 + subepithelial humps = PSGN

wrongOptions.explanation: Lupus nephritis is caused by immune complex deposition producing a “full-house” immunofluorescence pattern and wire-loop capillary thickening. Patients commonly have positive ANA and anti-dsDNA antibodies.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: SLE + wire-loop lesions + full-house immunofluorescence = Lupus nephritis

wrongOptions.explanation: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a small-vessel vasculitis associated with asthma, eosinophilia, and p-ANCA positivity
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Asthma + eosinophilia + p-ANCA = EGPA

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: c-ANCA + pauci-immune crescents + RPGN = Granulomatosis with polyangiitis

stem:
A 62-year-old woman on lisinopril due to hypertension for 3 years develops acute tongue and lip swelling without urticaria or pruritus. She has no prior allergic history. Which of the following best explains this reaction?

A) IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity to lisinopril
B) Bradykinin accumulation causing increased vascular permeability
C) Complement activation via the classical pathway
D) Direct mast cell degranulation without IgE sensitization
explanation: ACEi angioedema is bradykinin-mediated (non-allergic), not IgE-mediated. Bradykinin excess increases vascular permeability in deep dermal and submucosal tissues → non-pitting edema without urticaria. It can occur years after starting the drug, not just at initiation. Treatment: stop ACEi; B₂ receptor antagonist or C1-esterase inhibitor for severe cases. Epinephrine may help airway compromise but antihistamines and steroids are less effective (not histamine-mediated).
correctAnswerText: B) Bradykinin accumulation causing increased vascular permeability

choices.text: IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity to lisinopril
Bradykinin accumulation causing increased vascular permeability
Complement activation via the classical pathway
Direct mast cell degranulation without IgE sensitization

wrongOptions.explanation: IgE-mediated reactions require prior sensitization and cause urticaria, pruritus, and bronchospasm features absent here. ACEi angioedema is bradykinin-mediated (non-IgE), explaining why antihistamines and steroids are ineffective.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: IgE-mediated angioedema + urticaria + pruritus + bronchospasm = Type I hypersensitivity

wrongOptions.explanation: Complement-mediated angioedema occurs in hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency and C1q, C4, C2 consumption). ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema does not involve classical complement pathway activation.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: ↓ C4 + C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency + hereditary angioedema = Complement-mediated

wrongOptions.text: D) Direct mast cell degranulation without IgE
wrongOptions.explanation: Non-IgE mast cell degranulation (e.g., from opioids, vancomycin) releases histamine → urticaria + flushing. ACEi angioedema is not histamine driven it is bradykinin driven, which explains the lack of urticaria and poor response to antihistamines.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Vancomycin + urticaria + flushing = Direct mast cell degranulation (Non-IgE mast cell degranulation)

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: ACEi + tongue/lip swelling + no urticaria or pruritus = Bradykinin angioedema (not IgE-mediated)

stem:
A physiology student is reviewing the mechanisms of skeletal muscle relaxation during a laboratory session. During the lecture, the professor explains that after muscle contraction occurs, calcium ions must be transported from the cytoplasm back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum by the SERCA pump to allow relaxation of the muscle fiber. The professor emphasizes that this transport process is an example of active transport and requires a specific energy source to function properly.
Which of the following is directly required for SERCA pump activity in skeletal muscle?
explanation: SERCA (Sarcoplasmic/Endoplasmic Reticulum Ca2+-ATPase) is an ATP-dependent transport protein located in the membrane of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Its function is to actively pump calcium ions from the cytoplasm back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum after muscle contraction, allowing muscle relaxation to occur.

wrongOptions.explanation: Sodium ions are important in membrane depolarization and action potential generation, not direct SERCA pump function.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Membrane depolarization + action potentials + extracellular cation = sodium ions

wrongOptions.explanation: Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter released at the neuromuscular junction to initiate muscle contraction.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Neuromuscular junction + nicotinic receptors + muscle stimulation = acetylcholine

wrongOptions.explanation: Troponin binds calcium during muscle contraction and regulates tropomyosin movement.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Calcium binding + thin filament regulation + contraction initiation = troponin

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Calcium reuptake + active transport + sarcoplasmic reticulum = SERCA pump

stem:
A physiology student is studying skeletal muscle relaxation during a laboratory session. The professor explains that after muscle contraction, calcium ions must be rapidly transported from the cytoplasm back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum by the SERCA pump. During an experiment, a mutation causes defective SERCA function in skeletal muscle fibers.
Which of the following is the most likely consequence of this defect?
explanation: SERCA (Sarcoplasmic/Endoplasmic Reticulum Ca2+-ATPase) is responsible for actively transporting calcium ions from the cytoplasm back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum after muscle contraction. If SERCA is defective, calcium remains elevated in the cytoplasm, allowing continued actin-myosin interaction and impaired muscle relaxation.
correctAnswerText: A. Prolonged elevation of cytosolic calcium causing impaired muscle relaxation

choices.text: Prolonged elevation of cytosolic calcium causing impaired muscle relaxation
Inability of calcium to bind troponin C during contraction
Failure of acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
Decreased ATP hydrolysis by myosin heads during the power stroke

wrongOptions.text: B. Inability of calcium to bind troponin C during contraction
wrongOptions.explanation: Troponin C itself binds calcium normally; the problem is failure of calcium removal from the cytoplasm.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Calcium binding + thin filament regulation + contraction initiation = troponin C

wrongOptions.text: C. Failure of acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
wrongOptions.explanation: Acetylcholine release is mediated by presynaptic calcium-dependent vesicle fusion, not SERCA.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Neuromuscular transmission + synaptic vesicles + motor end plate = acetylcholine release

wrongOptions.text: D. Decreased ATP hydrolysis by myosin heads during the power stroke
wrongOptions.explanation: ATP hydrolysis during contraction is performed by myosin ATPase, not SERCA.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Power stroke + cross-bridge cycling + ATPase activity = myosin head

buzzwords: defective SERCA function in skeletal muscle fibers
buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Calcium reuptake defect + prolonged contraction + impaired relaxation = SERCA dysfunction
tags: defective SERCA function in skeletal muscle fibers

stem: An 18-year-old college student is brought to the emergency department after collapsing during a marathon. Her friends report that she drank massive amounts of water throughout the race to "stay hydrated." She is currently confused and disoriented. Laboratory studies show a serum sodium level of 118 mEq/L and a serum osmolality of 250 mOsm/kg. Urinalysis reveals a urine osmolality of 85 mOsm/kg and a urine sodium concentration of 12 mEq/L. Which of the following best explains the primary renal mechanism responsible for her condition?
explanation: The patient has psychogenic polydipsia/exercise-associated hyponatremia due to massive water intake that exceeds the kidney's maximum capacity to excrete free water (approximately 12 to 18 L/day). The appropriately low urine osmolality (less than 100 mOsm/kg) demonstrates that ADH is successfully suppressed, ruling out ADH-mediated water retention.

choices.text: Exceeding the renal capacity for free water excretion
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
Hypovolemia-induced activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
Decreased solute delivery to the diluting segments of the nephron

wrongOptions.text: B) Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
wrongOptions.explanation: SIADH would cause inappropriate water retention, but the urine osmolality would be inappropriately elevated (typically greater than 100 mOsm/kg, and often greater than serum osmolality) despite the hyponatremia.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Marathon runner + Hyponatremia + Inappropriately high urine osmolality = SIADH

wrongOptions.text: C) Hypovolemia-induced activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
wrongOptions.explanation: Hypovolemic hyponatremia occurs with significant volume depletion (e.g., severe vomiting/diarrhea), which triggers ADH release and leads to a high urine osmolality, unlike this patient's maximally dilute urine.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Dehydration + Low blood pressure + Concentrated urine = Hypovolemic hyponatremia

wrongOptions.text: D) Decreased solute delivery to the diluting segments of the nephron
wrongOptions.explanation: Decreased solute delivery to the diluting segments occurs in states of severe volume depletion or advanced chronic kidney disease, limiting the kidney's ability to dilute urine, which is not the case here given the urine osmolality of 85 mOsm/kg.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Advanced kidney disease + Low GFR + Inability to dilute urine = Decreased solute delivery to diluting segments

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Marathon runner + Massive water intake + Urine osmolality less than 100 mOsm/kg = Exceeding renal free water excretion capacity

stem: 24-year-old woman presents to the clinic complaining of muscle weakness and intermittent cramps. She admits to a long history of purging behaviors and restrictive eating. Physical examination shows dental erosions and parotid gland enlargement. Laboratory studies reveal a serum potassium level of 2.8 mEq/L, a serum bicarbonate level of 32 mEq/L, and a blood pressure of 98/60 mmHg. Urinalysis shows a urine chloride concentration of 8 mEq/L (normal is greater than 20 mEq/L). Which of the following renal physiological responses is most directly driving the maintenance of her metabolic alkalosis and worsening her hypokalemia?
explanation: Vomiting causes a loss of gastric HCl, leading to volume depletion and activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). High aldosterone levels promote sodium reabsorption in the principal cells, generating a negative lumen potential that drives potassium and hydrogen excretion, maintaining both the hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis.

choices.text: Increased hydrogen ion secretion via apical H+/K +-ATPase in the intercalated cells
Aldosterone-mediated sodium reabsorption in exchange for potassium and hydrogen secretion in the collecting duct
Direct inhibition of the Na/K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
Decreased proximal tubule reabsorption of bicarbonate due to volume expansion

wrongOptions.text: A) Increased hydrogen ion secretion via apical H+/K + -ATPase in alpha-intercalated cells
wrongOptions.explanation: severe hypokalemia, the H+/K + -ATPase in alpha-intercalated cells is actually upregulated to reabsorb potassium at the expense of secreting hydrogen ions, which contributes to the alkalosis but acts as a compensatory attempt to save potassium, rather than driving the potassium wasting.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Severe hypokalemia + Intercalated cell activation + Urinary acidification = H +/K +ATPase upregulation

wrongOptions.text: C) Direct inhibition of the Na+−K +−2Cl − cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
wrongOptions.explanation: Inhibition of the Na+−K +−2Cl − cotransporter describes the mechanism of loop diuretics (or Bartter syndrome), which would present with an elevated urine chloride concentration (greater than 20 mEq/L).
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Hypokalemia + Metabolic alkalosis + High urine chloride = Loop diuretic abuse / Bartter syndrome

wrongOptions.text: D) Decreased proximal tubule reabsorption of bicarbonate due to volume expansion
wrongOptions.explanation: The patient is volume-depleted, not volume-expanded; volume depletion actually increases proximal tubule reabsorption of bicarbonate via angiotensin II, which prevents the kidneys from excreting excess bicarbonate.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Volume expansion + Bicarbonate wasting + Normalization of pH = Contraction alkalosis reversal

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Vomiting + Low urine chloride + High aldosterone = RAAS-driven potassium/hydrogen wasting

stem: A 64-year-old man suddenly develops drooping of the right eyelid and double vision. On examination, the right eye is positioned “down and out” with a dilated pupil. He also has left-sided spastic hemiparesis involving the arm and leg. MRI reveals an infarct in the right midbrain.
explanation: Weber syndrome is caused by a midbrain infarction involving the oculomotor nerve fascicles and cerebral peduncle. CN III involvement causes ptosis, mydriasis, and a “down and out” eye, while corticospinal tract involvement causes contralateral hemiparesis.
topicName: Weber Syndrome (Midbrain stroke affecting oculomotor nerve fascicles and cerebral peduncle)

wrongOptions.explanation: The facial motor nucleus is located in the pons and lesions cause ipsilateral facial paralysis, not oculomotor deficits.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Bell palsy + hyperacusis + loss of forehead movement = Facial motor nucleus

wrongOptions.explanation: Vestibular nuclei lesions cause vertigo, nystagmus, nausea, and vomiting rather than eye deviation with pupillary dilation.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Vertigo + vomiting + nystagmus = Vestibular nuclei

wrongOptions.explanation: The nucleus ambiguus controls swallowing and phonation through CN IX and X. Lesions cause dysphagia and hoarseness.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Dysphagia + hoarseness + absent gag reflex = Nucleus ambiguus

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Down and out eye + blown pupil + contralateral hemiparesis = Oculomotor nerve fascicles
tags: Weber Syndrome (Midbrain stroke affecting oculomotor nerve fascicles and cerebral peduncle)

stem:
A 58-year-old man suddenly collapses and is brought to the emergency department. He is awake and able to blink vertically on command but cannot move his arms, legs, or lower face. Sensation is intact. MRI shows infarction of the ventral pons.

Which structure is most likely damaged?
explanation: Locked-in syndrome is caused by basilar artery infarction damaging the ventral pons. Bilateral corticospinal and corticobulbar tract injury causes quadriplegia and paralysis of lower cranial nerves while sparing consciousness and vertical eye movements.
topicName: Locked-in Syndrome (Basilar artery infarction affecting ventral pons)

wrongOptions.explanation: MLF lesions cause internuclear ophthalmoplegia with impaired adduction and nystagmus, not complete body paralysis with preserved consciousness.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Failure of adduction + abducting nystagmus + multiple sclerosis = Medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion

wrongOptions.explanation: Vestibular nuclei lesions produce vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and nystagmus rather than quadriplegia.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Vertigo + vomiting + nystagmus = Vestibular nuclei lesion

wrongOptions.explanation: Spinothalamic tract lesions cause loss of pain and temperature sensation contralaterally but do not produce locked-in syndrome.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Contralateral pain/temp loss + preserved vibration + spinal cord lesion = Spinothalamic tract damage

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Awake quadriplegic patient + preserved blinking + ventral pons lesion = Corticospinal and corticobulbar tract damage
tags: Locked-in Syndrome (Basilar artery infarction affecting ventral pons)

stem:
A 61-year-old vegetarian man presents with progressive difficulty walking and numbness in his feet. Examination shows impaired vibration and position sense in both lower extremities, spasticity, hyperreflexia, and a positive Babinski sign. Romberg test is positive. Laboratory testing reveals macrocytic anemia.

Which spinal cord tracts are most likely involved?
explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration involving the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts. This leads to loss of vibration/proprioception with concurrent upper motor neuron signs such as spasticity and Babinski reflexes.
topicName: Subacute Combined Degeneration (Dorsal column and corticospinal tract degeneration due to vitamin B12 deficiency)
correctAnswerText: B) Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts

choices.text: Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts

wrongOptions.explanation: Spinothalamic tract lesions primarily cause pain and temperature deficits, which are not the dominant findings here.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Pain/temp loss + contralateral sensory deficit + anterior white commissure = Spinothalamic tract lesion

wrongOptions.explanation: Spinocerebellar tract lesions cause ataxia without the marked vibration loss and UMN findings seen in B12 deficiency.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Ataxic gait + dysmetria + cerebellar dysfunction = Spinocerebellar tract lesion

wrongOptions.explanation: Anterior horn cell lesions cause lower motor neuron findings such as fasciculations and hyporeflexia, not spasticity and dorsal column deficits.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Muscle atrophy + fasciculations + hyporeflexia = Anterior horn cell lesion

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Macrocytic anemia + vibration loss + UMN signs = Dorsal columns and corticospinal tract degeneration
tags: Subacute Combined Degeneration (Dorsal column and corticospinal tract degeneration due to vitamin B12 deficiency)

stem:
A 56-year-old man presents with progressive weakness in his hands and legs over the past year. Examination shows muscle atrophy, fasciculations, spasticity, hyperreflexia, and bilateral Babinski signs. Sensory examination is normal.

Degeneration of which spinal cord tract is responsible for this patient’s upper motor neuron findings?
explanation: The lateral corticospinal tract carries descending upper motor neuron fibers responsible for voluntary movement. Degeneration causes spasticity, hyperreflexia, and Babinski signs, which are classic UMN findings seen in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
topicName: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (Degeneration of lateral corticospinal tract and anterior horn cells)

wrongOptions.explanation: Dorsal column lesions produce loss of vibration and proprioception with sensory ataxia, not UMN motor findings.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Positive Romberg + vibration loss + sensory ataxia = Dorsal column lesion

wrongOptions.explanation: Spinothalamic tract lesions cause pain and temperature sensory deficits rather than spastic weakness.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Pain/temp loss + contralateral sensory deficit + cord lesion = Spinothalamic tract lesion

wrongOptions.explanation: Spinocerebellar tract lesions lead to ataxia and impaired unconscious proprioception, not Babinski signs or spasticity.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Ataxia + dysmetria + unsteady gait = Spinocerebellar tract lesion

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Spasticity + hyperreflexia + Babinski sign = Lateral corticospinal tract degeneration
tags: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (Degeneration of lateral corticospinal tract and anterior horn cells)

stem: A patient is diagnosed with clear cell renal cell carcinoma after presenting with hematuria and a renal mass. Which of the following genetic abnormalities is most strongly associated with this malignancy?
explanation: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma is strongly associated with loss of the VHL tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3p. Loss of VHL function increases hypoxia-inducible factor activity, promoting angiogenesis and tumor growth through increased VEGF production.
correctAnswerText: C) Deletion of the VHL tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3

choices.text: Mutation of the APC gene on chromosome 5
Mutation of the CFTR gene on chromosome 7
Deletion of the VHL tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3

wrongOptions.text: Mutation of the APC gene on chromosome 5
wrongOptions.explanation: Familial adenomatous polyposis is caused by APC mutations and is strongly associated with numerous colonic adenomatous polyps and colorectal carcinoma. APC normally regulates β-catenin degradation within the Wnt signaling pathway.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: APC mutation + colon polyps + colorectal cancer = FAP

wrongOptions.text: Mutation of the CFTR gene on chromosome 7
wrongOptions.explanation: Cystic fibrosis results from CFTR mutations causing abnormal chloride transport and thick mucus secretions. Patients commonly develop recurrent pulmonary infections, pancreatic insufficiency, and bronchiectasis.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: CFTR mutation + Pancreatic Insufficiency  + recurrent lung infections = Cystic fibrosis

wrongOptions.explanation: Huntington disease is caused by CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion on chromosome 4. Patients classically develop chorea, psychiatric disturbances, and progressive neurodegeneration
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: CAG repeat expansion + chorea + caudate degeneration = Huntington disease

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Chromosome 3p deletion + increased VEGF + clear cell RCC = VHL mutation

stem: 62-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine 2.1 mg/dL) presents for a routine follow-up. He was recently started on lisinopril for hypertension and diabetic nephropathy. Laboratory studies today reveal a serum potassium level of 6.2 mEq/L (up from 4.6 mEq/L two months ago) and a serum bicarbonate level of 20 mEq/L. An ECG shows peaked T waves. Which of the following alterations in renal collecting duct physiology is primarily responsible for his hyperkalemia?
explanation: ACE inhibitors like lisinopril suppress aldosterone production. Because aldosterone normally upregulates the expression and activity of apical ENaC channels and basolateral Na+/K+ATPases in the principal cells of the cortical collecting duct, its absence reduces the lumen-negative electrical potential required to secrete potassium into the urine.

choices.text: Decreased expression and activity of apical Epithelial Sodium Channels (ENaC)
Inhibition of the basolateral Na+/K +ATPase pump in the proximal convoluted tubule
Impaired intracellular shift of potassium driven by insulin deficiency
Reduced glomerular filtration rate leading to decreased absolute delivery of water to the loop of Henle

wrongOptions.text:
B) Inhibition of the basolateral Na+/K +
 -ATPase pump in the proximal convoluted tubule
wrongOptions.explanation: The primary site of aldosterone-regulated potassium excretion is the principal cells of the late distal tubule and cortical collecting duct, not the proximal convoluted tubule.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Proximal tubule dysfunction + Bicarbonate wasting + Glucosuria = Fanconi syndrome

wrongOptions.text: C) Impaired intracellular shift of potassium driven by insulin deficiency
wrongOptions.explanation: While insulin deficiency can cause hyperkalemia by reducing the cellular uptake of potassium via Na+/K +-ATPase in skeletal muscle, this represents a transcellular shift abnormality rather than a renal collecting duct physiologic mechanism.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Diabetic ketoacidosis + Lack of insulin + Extracellular potassium shift = Transcellular hyperkalemia

wrongOptions.text: D) Reduced glomerular filtration rate leading to decreased absolute delivery of water to the loop of Henle
wrongOptions.explanation: While a reduced GFR can limit absolute potassium filtration, hyperkalemia in patients on ACE inhibitors is specifically driven by a lack of distal tubule aldosterone action rather than simple changes in loop of Henle fluid delivery.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Acute renal failure + Oliguria + Complete lack of solute delivery = Oliguric hyperkalemia

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: ACE inhibitor + Hypoaldosteronism + Reduced principal cell negative potential = Decreased ENaC/Potassium excretion

stem: 55-year-old woman comes to the physician due to worsening fatigue, constipation, and mild bone pain over the past 3 months. Laboratory testing demonstrates a corrected serum calcium level of 11.4 mg/dL and a serum phosphorus level of 2.2 mg/dL. Her serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) level is elevated. In the kidneys, PTH works to correct calcium homeostasis. Which of the following details the exact location and transport mechanism upregulated by PTH to maximize calcium reabsorption?
explanation: PTH directly upregulates transcellular calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule (DCT) by increasing the opening probability of apical TRPV5 calcium channels. Calcium then diffuses across the cell and is pumped into the blood via basolateral Ca2+-ATPase and Na + /Ca 2+ exchangers.

choices.text: Apical Ca2+ channels (TRPV5) in the distal convoluted tubule
Paracellular passive diffusion driven by the positive lumen potential in the thick ascending limb

wrongOptions.explanation: The majority of renal calcium ( 60−70%) is reabsorbed paracellularly in the proximal tubule and thick ascending limb ( 20%), but this passive process is modulated by the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) and loop voltage, whereas PTH specifically regulates the active transcellular mechanism in the DCT.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Thick ascending limb + Positive lumen potential + Paracellular transport = Loop-diuretic sensitive calcium reabsorption

wrongOptions.explanation: The proximal convoluted tubule handles bulk calcium reabsorption passively alongside sodium and water; it is not the site of PTH-stimulated active calcium reabsorption, where PTH instead inhibits phosphate reabsorption.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Proximal tubule + PTH activation + Phosphate wasting = Inhibition of sodium-phosphate cotransport

wrongOptions.explanation:
The Na+−K+−2Cl −
  cotransporter creates the positive lumen charge that drives calcium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb, but it is not directly upregulated by PTH to actively extract calcium from the filtrate.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: NKCC2 cotransporter + Potassium recycling + Paracellular calcium drive = Thick ascending limb passive clearance

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Primary hyperparathyroidism + Distal convoluted tubule + Active transcellular transport = TRPV5 upregulation

stem: 34-year-old construction worker is brought to the emergency department after his lower extremities were pinned under a collapsed concrete wall for 4 hours. On arrival, he is alert but complains of severe leg pain. Physical examination reveals extensive bruising and tense swelling of both thighs. Laboratory studies show a serum creatinine of 1.9 mg/dL, a serum potassium level of 6.8 mEq/L, and a serum creatine kinase (CK) level of 45,000 U/L. An ECG shows peaked T waves and widening of the QRS complex. Which of the following cellular mechanisms is primarily responsible for the rapid development of this patient's hyperkalemia?
explanation: The patient is experiencing rhabdomyolysis from a crush injury, which causes direct mechanical and ischemic trauma to skeletal muscle cells. Because potassium is the primary intracellular cation, the subsequent lysis of the sarcolemma causes a massive, rapid release of intracellular potassium directly into the extracellular fluid space, overwhelming renal clearance.

choices.text: Mechanical rupture of cell membranes releasing intracellular ion stores
Ischemia-induced upregulation of the basolateral Na +/K +-ATPase pump
Metabolic alkalosis driving a transcellular hydrogen-potassium exchange
Acute secondary hyperaldosteronism causing profound renal cortical necrosis

wrongOptions.explanation:
Ischemia actually depletes cellular ATP, which inhibits the energy-dependent basolateral Na+/K +
 -ATPase pump. This inhibition prevents potassium from being pumped into cells, worsening the extracellular accumulation.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: ATP depletion + Failure to pump potassium inward + Cellular swelling = Na+/K +-ATPase pump failure

wrongOptions.explanation: Crush injuries and tissue ischemia lead to a severe metabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis), not alkalosis. Acidosis drives hydrogen ions into cells in exchange for potassium ions moving outward into the extracellular fluid, which exacerbates hyperkalemia.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Lactic acidosis + Extracellular hydrogen buffering + Transcellular shift out of cells = Acidosis-induced hyperkalemia

wrongOptions.explanation: Hyperaldosteronism would cause increased renal potassium excretion and hypokalemia, which directly contradicts this patient’s high serum potassium level.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: High aldosterone levels + Cortical collecting duct activation + Urinary potassium wasting = Hypokalemia

buzzwords: peaked T waves and widening QRS
buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Trauma/Crush injury + Markedly elevated creatine kinase + Severe hyperkalemia = Transcellular shift via rhabdomyolysis
tags: peaked T waves and widening QRS

stem: A patient with seizures and facial angiofibromas is found to have a renal mass containing fat and smooth muscle. Which of the following renal neoplasms is most strongly associated with this patient’s condition?
explanation: Renal angiomyolipoma is a benign renal tumor composed of blood vessels, smooth muscle, and adipose tissue. It is strongly associated with tuberous sclerosis complex and may present with flank pain, hematuria, or spontaneous hemorrhage.

wrongOptions.explanation: Wilms tumor is a malignant renal tumor of childhood associated with WT1 mutations. It typically presents as an abdominal mass in young children rather than adults with tuberous sclerosis
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Childhood renal mass + WT1 mutation + nephroblastoma = Wilms tumor

wrongOptions.explanation: Urothelial carcinoma is associated with smoking and aromatic amine exposure. Patients commonly present with painless hematuria arising from the bladder or renal pelvis urothelium
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Smoking + painless hematuria + amine exposure = Urothelial carcinoma

wrongOptions.explanation: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma is associated with VHL gene abnormalities on chromosome 3p and originates from renal tubular epithelium. It commonly presents with hematuria, flank pain, and paraneoplastic syndromes
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: VHL mutation + renal cortical tumor + VEGF overexpression = Clear cell RCC

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Angiofibromas + Angiomyolipoma + smooth muscle proliferation = Tuberous sclerosis

stem: A patient with hematuria, hypertension, and edema develops renal disease several weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis. Which of the following renal disorders is most strongly associated with this presentation?
explanation: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis occurs after streptococcal pharyngitis or skin infection and presents with nephritic syndrome including hematuria, hypertension, edema, and red blood cell casts. The disease is caused by immune complex deposition with low complement levels and subepithelial hump-shaped deposits

wrongOptions.explanation: Minimal change disease is most commonly associated with children. It is characterized by diffuse podocyte foot process effacement with normal light microscopy
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Childhood nephrotic syndrome + podocyte effacement = Minimal change disease

wrongOptions.explanation: Membranous nephropathy is associated with hepatitis B infection, solid tumors, systemic lupus erythematosus, and anti-PLA2R antibodies. The disease is characterized by subepithelial immune complex deposition and thickened glomerular basement membranes
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Subepithelial deposits + spike-and-dome appearance = Membranous nephropathy

wrongOptions.explanation: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is strongly associated with HIV infection, heroin use, obesity, and sickle cell disease. Patients commonly develop nephrotic-range proteinuria and progressive renal dysfunction
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: HIV + heroin use + Proteinuria = FSGS

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Recent streptococcal infection + cola-colored urine + Subepithelial Humps = PSGN

stem: A patient develops severe edema, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, and 4+ proteinuria on urinalysis. Which of the following complications is most likely to occur in this patient?
explanation: Nephrotic syndrome causes urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins such as antithrombin III, creating a hypercoagulable state. Patients are therefore at increased risk for thrombotic complications, particularly renal vein thrombosis

wrongOptions.explanation: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage is more commonly associated with pulmonary-renal syndromes such as Goodpasture syndrome and ANCA-associated vasculitis. Patients typically present with hemoptysis, anemia, and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Hemoptysis + glomerulonephritis + pulmonary infiltrates = Pulmonary-renal syndrome

wrongOptions.explanation: Splenic sequestration crisis is associated with sickle cell disease and acute trapping of red blood cells within the spleen. Patients develop sudden splenomegaly, anemia, and hypovolemic shock
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Sickle cell disease + acute splenomegaly + hypovolemia = Splenic sequestration

wrongOptions.explanation: Subarachnoid hemorrhage is classically caused by rupture of a berry aneurysm. Patients typically present with sudden severe “thunderclap” headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Berry aneurysm rupture + thunderclap headache + meningeal irritation = Subarachnoid hemorrhage

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Proteinuria + antithrombin III loss + hypercoagulability = Renal vein thrombosis

stem: Which of the following diseases is most strongly associated with linear IgG deposition along the glomerular basement membrane and hemoptysis?
explanation: Goodpasture syndrome is caused by antibodies directed against type IV collagen in the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes. Patients classically develop rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with hematuria and pulmonary hemorrhage.

wrongOptions.explanation: IgA nephropathy is associated with mesangial IgA deposition and recurrent hematuria occurring shortly after upper respiratory infections
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: URI + hematuria + mesangial IgA = IgA nephropathy

wrongOptions.explanation: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis occurs after streptococcal infection and is characterized by low complement levels and subepithelial hump-shaped deposits.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Recent strep infection + low C3 + subepithelial humps = PSGN

wrongOptions.explanation: Membranous nephropathy is a nephrotic syndrome associated with subepithelial immune complex deposition producing a spike-and-dome appearance.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Nephrotic syndrome + spike-and-dome deposits = Membranous nephropathy

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Hemoptysis + RPGN + linear IgG = Goodpasture syndrome

stem: A patient develops hematuria, renal biopsy demonstrates crescent formation with minimal immune complex deposition, and serology is positive for c-ANCA. Which of the following diseases is most strongly associated with this presentation?
explanation: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotizing vasculitis associated with positive c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA) antibodies. Patients commonly develop rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis with little or no immune complex deposition on immunofluorescence, producing a pauci-immune pattern.

wrongOptions.explanation: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immune complex–mediated nephritic syndrome associated with low complement levels and subepithelial hump-shaped deposits after streptococcal infection.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Recent strep infection + low C3 + subepithelial humps = PSGN

wrongOptions.explanation: Lupus nephritis is caused by immune complex deposition producing a “full-house” immunofluorescence pattern and wire-loop capillary thickening. Patients commonly have positive ANA and anti-dsDNA antibodies.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: SLE + wire-loop lesions + full-house immunofluorescence = Lupus nephritis

wrongOptions.explanation: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a small-vessel vasculitis associated with asthma, eosinophilia, and p-ANCA positivity
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Asthma + eosinophilia + p-ANCA = EGPA

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: c-ANCA + pauci-immune crescents + RPGN = Granulomatosis with polyangiitis

stem:
A 62-year-old woman on lisinopril due to hypertension for 3 years develops acute tongue and lip swelling without urticaria or pruritus. She has no prior allergic history. Which of the following best explains this reaction?

A) IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity to lisinopril
B) Bradykinin accumulation causing increased vascular permeability
C) Complement activation via the classical pathway
D) Direct mast cell degranulation without IgE sensitization
explanation: ACEi angioedema is bradykinin-mediated (non-allergic), not IgE-mediated. Bradykinin excess increases vascular permeability in deep dermal and submucosal tissues → non-pitting edema without urticaria. It can occur years after starting the drug, not just at initiation. Treatment: stop ACEi; B₂ receptor antagonist or C1-esterase inhibitor for severe cases. Epinephrine may help airway compromise but antihistamines and steroids are less effective (not histamine-mediated).
correctAnswerText: B) Bradykinin accumulation causing increased vascular permeability

choices.text: IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity to lisinopril
Bradykinin accumulation causing increased vascular permeability
Complement activation via the classical pathway
Direct mast cell degranulation without IgE sensitization

wrongOptions.explanation: IgE-mediated reactions require prior sensitization and cause urticaria, pruritus, and bronchospasm features absent here. ACEi angioedema is bradykinin-mediated (non-IgE), explaining why antihistamines and steroids are ineffective.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: IgE-mediated angioedema + urticaria + pruritus + bronchospasm = Type I hypersensitivity

wrongOptions.explanation: Complement-mediated angioedema occurs in hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency and C1q, C4, C2 consumption). ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema does not involve classical complement pathway activation.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: ↓ C4 + C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency + hereditary angioedema = Complement-mediated

wrongOptions.text: D) Direct mast cell degranulation without IgE
wrongOptions.explanation: Non-IgE mast cell degranulation (e.g., from opioids, vancomycin) releases histamine → urticaria + flushing. ACEi angioedema is not histamine driven it is bradykinin driven, which explains the lack of urticaria and poor response to antihistamines.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Vancomycin + urticaria + flushing = Direct mast cell degranulation (Non-IgE mast cell degranulation)

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: ACEi + tongue/lip swelling + no urticaria or pruritus = Bradykinin angioedema (not IgE-mediated)

stem: A young woman repeatedly checks mirrors and excessively applies makeup because she believes her nose is severely deformed, although others perceive her appearance as normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: BDD is characterized by excessive preoccupation with perceived appearance flaws accompanied by repetitive behaviors such as mirror checking and grooming. The perceived defect is usually minimal or not observable to others.

wrongOptions.explanation: Anorexia nervosa centers on distorted perceptions of weight and body size with restrictive eating behaviors, not isolated concerns about facial appearance.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Fear of weight gain + restrictive eating + low BMI = Anorexia nervosa

wrongOptions.explanation: Social anxiety disorder involves fear of embarrassment in social settings rather than obsessive appearance-focused behaviors.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Fear of public embarrassment + avoidance + performance anxiety = Social anxiety disorder

wrongOptions.explanation: BDD patients often have repetitive compulsive behaviors focused on appearance, unlike isolated fixed delusions without compulsions.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Fixed false belief + preserved functioning + nonbizarre delusion = Delusional disorder

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Perceived appearance flaw + mirror checking + excessive grooming = BDD

stem: A patient with body dysmorphic disorder asks for repeated cosmetic procedures to “fix” a minor perceived defect. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: First-line treatment for BDD includes cognitive behavioral therapy and SSRIs. Cosmetic interventions are generally not recommended because they rarely improve the underlying psychiatric condition.
correctAnswerText: B. Cognitive behavioral therapy and SSRIs

wrongOptions.explanation: Cosmetic procedures typically do not relieve the obsessive preoccupation in BDD and may worsen symptoms.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Perceived cosmetic flaw + repeated procedures + persistent dissatisfaction = BDD cosmetic-seeking behavior

wrongOptions.explanation: Benzodiazepines may reduce anxiety temporarily but are not effective primary treatments for BDD.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Acute anxiety + rapid sedation + panic symptoms = Benzodiazepines

wrongOptions.explanation: ECT is primarily used for severe mood disorders and catatonia, not uncomplicated BDD.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Severe depression + suicidality + catatonia = ECT indication

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: BDD + repetitive appearance concerns + first-line treatment = CBT + SSRIs

stem: Drunk-like gait, truncal ataxia, vertigo, horizontal nystagmus, inability to maintain balance while standing, preserved limb coordination, and lesion of the vestibulocerebellum projecting through the fastigial nucleus most strongly indicate damage to which cerebellar region?
explanation: The flocculonodular lobe is the vestibulocerebellum and is responsible for balance and eye movements. Lesions cause truncal ataxia, vertigo, and nystagmus with relatively preserved limb coordination.
topicName: Flocculonodular lobe (vestibulocerebellum) lesion involving fastigial nucleus

wrongOptions.explanation: Dentate nucleus lesions produce intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, and limb ataxia due to impaired motor planning. Balance and vestibular symptoms are less prominent.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Intention tremor + dysdiadochokinesia + scanning speech = Dentate nucleus lesion

wrongOptions.explanation: Interposed nuclei (emboliform and globose) are associated with limb movement correction and cause ipsilateral limb ataxia rather than predominant truncal instability.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Limb ataxia + movement correction deficit + intermediate hemisphere lesion = Interposed nuclei

wrongOptions.explanation: The lateral cerebellar hemisphere coordinates skilled voluntary movement and motor planning. Lesions typically cause limb coordination deficits rather than isolated balance dysfunction.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Intention tremor + impaired motor planning + dysdiadochokinesia = Lateral cerebellar hemisphere lesion

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Vertigo + truncal ataxia + nystagmus = Flocculonodular lobe lesion
tags: Flocculonodular lobe (vestibulocerebellum) lesion involving fastigial nucleus

stem: Ipsilateral intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, limb ataxia, “drunk-like” coordination, lesion involving the major cerebellar output pathway that decussates in the midbrain and carries fibers from the dentate nucleus most strongly indicates damage to which structure?
explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle is the primary efferent pathway from the cerebellum carrying fibers from the dentate nucleus to the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus. Lesions produce ipsilateral cerebellar signs such as intention tremor and limb ataxia.

wrongOptions.explanation: The inferior cerebellar peduncle mainly carries afferent vestibular and spinocerebellar inputs to the cerebellum. Lesions are more associated with balance and vestibular dysfunction.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Vestibular input + spinocerebellar fibers + balance dysfunction = Inferior cerebellar peduncle

wrongOptions.explanation: The middle cerebellar peduncle carries pontocerebellar afferent fibers from the contralateral cortex. It is the major input pathway to the cerebellum rather than the main output tract.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Pontine nuclei + cortical input + afferent cerebellar pathway = Middle cerebellar peduncle

wrongOptions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus coordinates conjugate eye movements between cranial nerve nuclei. Lesions classically cause internuclear ophthalmoplegia rather than cerebellar ataxia.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Diplopia + impaired adduction + internuclear ophthalmoplegia = Medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Dentate nucleus + cerebellar efferent fibers + midbrain decussation = Superior cerebellar peduncle

stem: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures, weight gain, hair loss, easy bruising, elevated liver enzymes, pancreatitis, teratogenic anticonvulsant that blocks Na⁺ channels, T-type Ca²⁺ channels, and GABA transaminase most strongly indicates toxicity from which medication?
explanation: Valproate is a broad-spectrum anticonvulsant that blocks Na⁺ channels, T-type Ca²⁺ channels, and GABA transaminase. Classic adverse effects include hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, weight gain, hair loss, thrombocytopenia/easy bruising, and teratogenicity.

wrongOptions.explanation: Ethosuximide is used only for absence seizures and commonly causes fatigue, sedation, and GI upset. It is not associated with pancreatitis or major hepatotoxicity.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Absence seizures + T-type Ca²⁺ blockade + GI distress = Ethosuximide

wrongOptions.explanation: Topiramate commonly causes kidney stones, paresthesias, cognitive slowing, and weight loss. Weight gain and pancreatitis are not classic features.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Kidney stones + weight loss + angle-closure glaucoma = Topiramate

wrongOptions.explanation: Levetiracetam acts through SV2A synaptic vesicle protein modulation and is notable for mood and behavioral disturbances rather than hepatotoxicity and pancreatitis.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Psychosis + irritability + SV2A binding = Levetiracetam

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Pancreatitis + weight gain + hair loss = Valproate

stem: Focal and generalized seizures, minimal drug interactions, fatigue, dizziness, behavioral changes, irritability, psychosis, anticonvulsant acting through synaptic vesicle modulation most strongly corresponds to which mechanism of action?
explanation: Levetiracetam works by binding synaptic vesicle protein 2A (SV2A), which modulates neurotransmitter release. It is commonly associated with neuropsychiatric adverse effects such as irritability, agitation, and psychosis.
correctAnswerText: C) Binds synaptic vesicle protein SV2A

wrongOptions.explanation: Na⁺ channel blockade is the mechanism of drugs such as phenytoin, carbamazepine, and lamotrigine. These drugs are more associated with rash, diplopia, and DRESS/SJS.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Diplopia + gingival hyperplasia + CYP450 induction = Na⁺ channel blockade

wrongOptions.explanation: T-type Ca²⁺ channel blockade is characteristic of ethosuximide, which is primarily used for absence seizures.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Absence seizures + 3-Hz spike-wave + T-type Ca²⁺ blockade = Ethosuximide MOA

wrongOptions.explanation: Valproate inhibits GABA transaminase and increases CNS GABA levels. It is associated with hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, and neural tube defects.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Pancreatitis + weight gain + teratogenicity = GABA transaminase inhibition

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Psychosis + minimal drug interactions + synaptic vesicle modulation = SV2A binding

stem:
A 29-year-old woman with hypertension and chronic kidney disease is started on lisinopril. She returns 6 weeks later pregnant at 8 weeks gestation. Which of the following best describes the fetal risk of continuing lisinopril?

A) Fetal cardiac septal defects
B) Fetal renal tubular dysgenesis
C) Neonatal hyperthyroidism
D) Neural tube defects
explanation: ACE inhibitors are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. Fetal angiotensin II is essential for normal renal development and perfusion. ACEi blockade of fetal RAAS → fetal renal tubular dysgenesis → ↓ urine output → oligohydramnios → Potter sequence complications: pulmonary hypoplasia (from oligohydramnios), skull hypoplasia, limb contractures, intrauterine growth restriction, and renal failure.

wrongOptions.explanation: While first-trimester ACEi exposure has been associated with increased cardiac defects in some studies, the most established and severe teratogenic effect is fetal renal tubular dysgenesis
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Lithium + pregnancy = Ebstein anomaly and septal defects.

wrongOptions.explanation: ACE inhibitors have no effect on thyroid ACE receptors or thyroid function. Neonatal thyroid disease is associated with maternal antithyroid antibodies (Graves)
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Neonatal hyperthyroidism + maternal Graves = TSH receptor antibody crossing placenta

wrongOptions.explanation: Neural tube defects are associated with folate deficiency and antiepileptic drugs not ACE inhibitors. ACEi has no mechanism for folate depletion
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Valproate + pregnancy = Neural tube defects

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: ACEi + pregnancy = Fetal renal failure

stem: A medical student is reviewing a glucose titration curve and notices that glucosuria begins at a plasma glucose of ~180 mg/dL in one nephron, but not until ~220 mg/dL in another. The overall curve shows a gradual rather than sharp rise in excreted glucose before the transport maximum (Tₘ) is reached. Which of the following best describes the mechanism responsible for this gradual rise?
explanation: The splay phenomenon occurs because individual nephrons have slightly different transport maximums. Some nephrons saturate and spill glucose at lower plasma glucose levels while others continue reabsorbing, creating a gradual rather than sharp inflection on the titration curve between the renal threshold and the overall Tₘ.

choices.text: Downregulation of SGLT2 transporters at high glucose concentrations
Saturation of all nephron transporters simultaneously at the renal threshold
Variable Tₘ across individual nephrons due to differing transporter capacities
Increased GFR overwhelming a single uniform transport maximum

wrongOptions.text: B) Simultaneous saturation at renal threshold
wrongOptions.explanation: This is the premature closure trap — students assume all nephrons behave identically and saturate at once, which would produce a sharp rise. The splay exists precisely because nephrons are NOT uniform in their transport capacity.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Renal threshold + all nephrons saturate together = sharp rise (not splay)

wrongOptions.explanation: SGLT2 transporters are not downregulated by high glucose concentrations under physiologic conditions. The splay is a structural/anatomical phenomenon related to nephron heterogeneity, not transporter regulation.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: High glucose + SGLT2 change = splay (incorrect mechanism)

wrongOptions.text: D) Increased GFR overwhelming uniform Tₘ
wrongOptions.explanation: Increased GFR shifts the threshold leftward (as in pregnancy) but does not create the gradual splay pattern. Splay is specifically due to inter-nephron variability in Tₘ, not a GFR-driven phenomenon.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: ↑GFR + uniform Tₘ = splay (incorrect — GFR affects threshold, not splay)

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Nephron heterogeneity + different Tₘ points + gradual curve = Splay phenomenon

stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman at 32 weeks gestation is found to have glucose in her urine on routine dipstick. Her fasting plasma glucose is 85 mg/dL and HbA1c is 5.1%. Which of the following best explains this finding?
explanation: Normal pregnancy increases GFR, which increases filtered glucose load. This causes the renal threshold for glucosuria to occur at lower plasma glucose concentrations, resulting in glucosuria despite normal blood glucose levels.

choices.text: Decreased renal glucose reabsorption due to tubular damage
Increased GFR lowers the plasma glucose threshold for glucosuria

wrongOptions.explanation: This is the classic premature closure trap — glucosuria in pregnancy immediately suggests GDM, but her fasting glucose and HbA1c are completely normal, ruling out diabetes as the cause.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Glucosuria + pregnancy = GDM (incorrect without hyperglycemia)

wrongOptions.explanation: There is no clinical history suggesting tubular injury (no toxin exposure, no Fanconi features). Pregnancy-associated glucosuria is physiologic, not pathologic.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Glucosuria + pregnancy = tubular damage (incorrect — physiologic mechanism)

wrongOptions.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors pharmacologically block reabsorption, but pregnancy does not downregulate SGLT2 receptors. The mechanism is hemodynamic (↑GFR), not transporter-based.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Glucosuria + pregnancy = SGLT2 dysfunction (incorrect mechanism)

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Pregnancy + ↑GFR + normal glucose = glucosuria at lower threshold

stem: A 31-year-old woman at 28 weeks gestation presents for routine prenatal care. Urine dipstick shows 2+ glucose. Fasting plasma glucose is 82 mg/dL and a 75g OGTT shows a 1-hour value of 155 mg/dL and 2-hour value of 128 mg/dL. Serum electrolytes, phosphate, uric acid, and amino acids are all normal. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism for her glucosuria?
explanation: Pregnancy physiologically increases GFR and renal plasma flow, increasing the filtered glucose load. This causes the renal threshold to be reached at lower plasma glucose concentrations, producing glucosuria despite completely normal glucose tolerance testing. Normal amino acids and electrolytes rule out global tubular dysfunction.

choices.text: Defective SGLT2 transporter causing isolated renal glucosuria
Increased GFR reducing the plasma glucose concentration at which renal threshold is reached
Global PCT dysfunction impairing reabsorption of glucose and other solutes
Pancreatic beta-cell insufficiency causing intermittent postprandial hyperglycemia

wrongOptions.explanation: Fanconi syndrome causes glucosuria alongside phosphaturia, aminoaciduria, uricosuria, and renal tubular acidosis — a global reabsorption defect. This patient has isolated glucosuria with all other solutes normal, making Fanconi incorrect.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Glucosuria + normal amino acids + normal phosphate = NOT Fanconi

wrongOptions.explanation: A finding of isolated glucosuria at normal plasma glucose could suggest a congenital SGLT2 defect, but the clinical context of pregnancy with its known hemodynamic changes makes physiologic GFR elevation the far more likely explanation.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Isolated glucosuria + normal glucose = SGLT2 defect (incorrect in pregnant patient without family history)

wrongOptions.explanation: Her OGTT values fall below diagnostic thresholds for GDM (1-hour <180, 2-hour <153 mg/dL by IADPSG criteria), ruling out beta-cell dysfunction as the mechanism. Glucosuria with a normal OGTT points away from hyperglycemia-driven spillage.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Glucosuria + pregnancy = GDM (incorrect — OGTT values normal)

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Pregnancy + ↑GFR + normal OGTT + normal amino acids = physiologic glucosuria (lowered threshold)

stem: A 19-year-old man is evaluated for glucosuria found incidentally on a routine sports physical. He is non-diabetic with a fasting glucose of 79 mg/dL. Further workup reveals: glucosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, and uricosuria. Serum bicarbonate is 18 mEq/L. He takes no medications. Which of the following best explains why this patient has glucosuria despite a normal plasma glucose?
explanation: The constellation of glucosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, uricosuria, and non-anion gap metabolic acidosis (low bicarb) in a young patient is the classic fingerprint of Fanconi syndrome — global PCT dysfunction. Unlike pregnancy or SGLT2i, this affects all PCT reabsorption processes, not glucose selectively.

choices.text: Increased GFR overwhelming the transport maximum for glucose
SGLT2 inhibitor effect reducing the renal glucose threshold selectively
Global proximal tubule dysfunction impairing reabsorption of multiple solutes
Splay phenomenon causing early saturation of glucose transporters

wrongOptions.explanation: Increased GFR (as in pregnancy) causes isolated glucosuria by lowering the threshold, but does NOT cause aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, or metabolic acidosis. The multi-solute loss here clearly implicates a tubular defect, not a hemodynamic one.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: ↑GFR = isolated glucosuria only, NOT multi-solute wasting

wrongOptions.explanation: Splay phenomenon explains the gradual rise in the glucose titration curve due to nephron heterogeneity, but it does not cause aminoaciduria or phosphaturia. Splay is a glucose-specific transport phenomenon.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Splay = glucose titration curve only, NOT global solute wasting

wrongOptions.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors cause selective glucosuria by blocking glucose reabsorption in the PCT, but they do not impair amino acid, phosphate, or bicarbonate reabsorption. This patient takes no medications, and the multi-solute loss pattern excludes a selective transporter block.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: SGLT2i = selective glucosuria only + patient takes no medications

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Glucosuria + aminoaciduria + phosphaturia + low bicarb + normal glucose = Fanconi syndrome (global PCT dysfunction)

stem: A 45-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is started on empagliflozin. Two weeks later, his fasting plasma glucose is 210 mg/dL and repeat urine dipstick shows 3+ glucose. His physician notes that prior to starting empagliflozin, at the same plasma glucose of 210 mg/dL, his urine dipstick showed only trace glucose. Which of the following best accounts for the increased glucosuria on empagliflozin compared to before treatment at the same plasma glucose level?
explanation: Empagliflozin inhibits SGLT2, which is responsible for ~90% of renal glucose reabsorption. By blocking SGLT2, the renal glucose threshold is pharmacologically lowered to below 210 mg/dL, so glucose that was previously reabsorbed is now excreted — even though plasma glucose is unchanged. This is a transporter-level shift in threshold, not a GFR or filtration change.

choices.text: Empagliflozin increases GFR, raising the filtered glucose load
Empagliflozin blocks SGLT2, lowering the renal glucose threshold below 210 mg/dL
Empagliflozin saturates SGLT1 in the PCT, eliminating secondary glucose reabsorption
Empagliflozin causes splay phenomenon by creating heterogeneity among SGLT2 transporters

wrongOptions.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors actually have a modest effect of slightly reducing intraglomerular pressure via tubuloglomerular feedback, but this is not the mechanism of glucosuria. More importantly, increased GFR would increase filtered load but not necessarily overcome reabsorption unless the threshold is also changed.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: SGLT2i + ↑GFR = glucosuria (incorrect primary mechanism)

wrongOptions.explanation: This is a wrong option choice as SGLT1 handles ~10% of glucose reabsorption in the S3 segment and is NOT blocked by empagliflozin. SGLT1 remains functional and continues reabsorbing residual glucose. The primary mechanism is SGLT2 blockade in S1/S2, not SGLT1 saturation.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Empagliflozin + SGLT1 blocked = incorrect (empagliflozin is SGLT2-selective)

wrongOptions.text: D) Splay phenomenon from SGLT2 heterogeneity
wrongOptions.explanation: Splay is an intrinsic anatomical phenomenon due to natural nephron-to-nephron variability in Tₘ — it exists in all individuals regardless of drug therapy. Empagliflozin does not create new heterogeneity among transporters; it uniformly inhibits SGLT2 across nephrons, shifting the entire threshold curve leftward.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Empagliflozin + splay = incorrect (splay is pre-existing, not drug-induced)

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Empagliflozin + SGLT2 block + same plasma glucose + more glucosuria = lowered renal threshold

stem: The posteromedial papillary muscle is the most common site of post-MI rupture because of which feature of its blood supply?
explanation: The posteromedial papillary muscle receives blood from only the posterior descending artery (a branch of the RCA in right-dominant circulations). This single blood supply makes it uniquely vulnerable to ischemic rupture after inferior MI. The anterolateral papillary muscle, in contrast, has dual blood supply from the LAD and LCX and rarely ruptures.

stem: A patient dies 5 days after a myocardial infarction from acute mitral regurgitation due to a transected papillary muscle. Histologic examination of the adjacent infarcted myocardium is most likely to show.
explanation: Days 3–7 post-MI are dominated by macrophage-mediated phagocytosis of necrotic myocytes, producing gross yellow softening of the infarcted tissue. This is when the myocardium is mechanically weakest, which is why mechanical complications — papillary muscle rupture, ventricular free wall rupture, and interventricular septal rupture — cluster in this window. The patient's papillary muscle transection on day 5 places him squarely in this peak rupture period.

Dense fibrous scar with type I collagen

wrongOptions.explanation: Days 7–10 post-MI; mechanical strength is beginning to be restored and rupture risk declines.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Day 7–10 + granulation tissue + type III collagen = healing phase

wrongOptions.text: Dense fibrous scar with type I collagen
wrongOptions.explanation: Weeks to months post-MI; represents complete healing and is the substrate for late complications such as ventricular aneurysm, not acute rupture.

explanation: Alpha-2 receptor agonists such as clonidine and guanfacine are commonly used in Tourette syndrome and may also improve comorbid ADHD symptoms.

wrongOptions.explanation: SSRIs are mainly used for anxiety and OCD symptoms rather than primary tic suppression.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Obsessions + compulsions + serotonin reuptake inhibition = SSRIs

wrongOptions.explanation: Benzodiazepines are not first-line therapy for chronic tic disorders.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Acute anxiety + panic symptoms + GABA enhancement = Benzodiazepines

wrongOptions.explanation: Cholinesterase inhibitors are used in dementia disorders such as Alzheimer disease, not Tourette syndrome.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Memory loss + dementia + acetylcholine enhancement = Cholinesterase inhibitors

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Tourette syndrome + ADHD + tic suppression = Alpha-2 receptor agonists

stem: A young child with a history of severe neglect rarely seeks comfort from caregivers, shows minimal emotional responsiveness, and appears fearful even in safe situations. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Reactive attachment disorder is caused by severe neglect or inconsistent caregiving and presents with emotionally withdrawn behavior and failure to seek comfort from caregivers.

wrongOptions.explanation: Autism spectrum disorder includes social communication deficits and repetitive behaviors but is not directly caused by neglect.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Restricted interests + repetitive behaviors + impaired social communication = Autism spectrum disorder

wrongOptions.explanation: Social anxiety disorder involves fear of embarrassment or judgment during social interactions.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Fear of scrutiny + avoidance of social situations + anxiety = Social anxiety disorder

wrongOptions.explanation: ODD presents with angry, defiant, and argumentative behavior rather than attachment disturbances.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Defiant behavior + irritability + argumentativeness = Oppositional defiant disorder

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Early neglect + withdrawn behavior + failure to seek comfort = Reactive attachment disorder

stem: A child with reactive attachment disorder is undergoing treatment. Which of the following is the most appropriate primary intervention?
explanation: The cornerstone of treatment for reactive attachment disorder is ensuring consistent, emotionally supportive caregiving to promote healthy attachment development.
correctAnswerText: A. Establishing a stable emotionally available caregiver

choices.text: Establishing a stable emotionally available caregiver

wrongOptions.explanation: Benzodiazepines are not first-line treatment and may worsen emotional and behavioral regulation.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Acute anxiety + sedation + GABA enhancement = Benzodiazepines

wrongOptions.explanation: ECT is not indicated for attachment disorders and is mainly used for severe mood disorders.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Severe depression + catatonia + refractory psychiatric illness = ECT

wrongOptions.explanation: Stimulants may help comorbid ADHD symptoms but do not address the underlying attachment disturbance.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Inattention + hyperactivity + dopamine/norepinephrine enhancement = Stimulants

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Attachment disorder + childhood neglect + treatment = Stable caregiver relationship

stem: An adolescent girl has patchy scalp hair loss with hairs of varying lengths and admits to repeatedly pulling out her hair during stressful situations. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Trichotillomania presents with compulsive hair pulling leading to patchy alopecia with irregular hairs of different lengths, commonly triggered by stress.

wrongOptions.explanation: Alopecia areata causes smooth circular patches of hair loss without evidence of broken hairs.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Smooth bald patches + autoimmune disease + exclamation point hairs = Alopecia areata

wrongOptions.explanation: Tinea capitis is a fungal scalp infection associated with scaling and inflammation.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Scalp scaling + fungal infection + cervical lymphadenopathy = Tinea capitis

wrongOptions.explanation: OCD involves intrusive thoughts and compulsions rather than isolated hair-pulling behavior.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Intrusive thoughts + repetitive rituals + anxiety relief = OCD

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Hair pulling + patchy alopecia + hairs of different lengths = Trichotillomania

stem: A patient with trichotillomania continues to have distressing hair-pulling behavior despite education and reassurance. Which of the following is considered first-line therapy?
explanation: Cognitive behavioral therapy with habit reversal training is the first-line treatment for trichotillomania. SSRIs have limited evidence of benefit.

wrongOptions.explanation: ECT is mainly used for severe mood disorders and catatonia, not trichotillomania.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Severe depression + catatonia + refractory psychiatric illness = ECT

wrongOptions.explanation: Lithium is primarily used as a mood stabilizer in bipolar disorder.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Mania + mood stabilization + suicide risk reduction = Lithium

wrongOptions.explanation: Benzodiazepines are not first-line therapy for compulsive hair-pulling disorders.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Acute anxiety + sedation + GABA enhancement = Benzodiazepines

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Trichotillomania + CBT + behavioral treatment = Habit reversal therapy

stem: A young adult with minimal smoking history develops lower-lobe panacinar emphysema and liver cirrhosis. Which condition is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency classically presents with early-onset lower-lobe panacinar emphysema and liver disease due to abnormal protein accumulation in hepatocytes.

wrongOptions.explanation: Chronic bronchitis is associated with chronic productive cough and smoking-related airway inflammation.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Productive cough + smoking + mucus hypersecretion = Chronic bronchitis

wrongOptions.explanation: Cystic fibrosis presents with recurrent pulmonary infections, pancreatic insufficiency, and bronchiectasis.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Bronchiectasis + pancreatic insufficiency + recurrent infections = Cystic fibrosis

wrongOptions.explanation: Sarcoidosis is characterized by noncaseating granulomas and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Noncaseating granulomas + hilar lymphadenopathy + elevated ACE = Sarcoidosis

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Lower-lobe emphysema + liver disease + young nonsmoker = Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

stem: A patient with severe alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency continues to have progressive COPD symptoms despite smoking cessation and bronchodilator therapy. Which treatment directly replaces the deficient protein?
explanation: IV augmentation therapy provides alpha-1 antitrypsin replacement and is indicated in individuals with severe deficiency.

wrongOptions.explanation: Inhaled corticosteroids may improve COPD symptoms but do not replace alpha-1 antitrypsin.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Airway inflammation + asthma/COPD + inhaled anti-inflammatory = Inhaled corticosteroids

wrongOptions.explanation: Surgery may help selected emphysema patients but does not correct the underlying deficiency.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Advanced emphysema + hyperinflation + surgical management = Lung volume reduction surgery

wrongOptions.explanation: Azithromycin may reduce COPD exacerbations but is not replacement therapy.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: COPD exacerbation prevention + anti-inflammatory antibiotic + chronic therapy = Azithromycin

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Severe AAT deficiency + replacement treatment + COPD = IV augmentation therapy

stem: An Ashkenazi Jewish infant develops developmental regression, exaggerated startle response, hypotonia, and a cherry-red macula without hepatosplenomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Tay-Sachs disease is caused by hexosaminidase A deficiency and classically presents with developmental regression, hyperacusis, cherry-red macula, and absence of hepatosplenomegaly.

wrongOptions.explanation: Niemann-Pick disease also causes a cherry-red spot but is associated with hepatosplenomegaly.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Cherry-red spot + hepatosplenomegaly + sphingomyelinase deficiency = Niemann-Pick disease

wrongOptions.explanation: Gaucher disease presents with hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and bone pain rather than hyperacusis.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Bone crises + hepatosplenomegaly + glucocerebrosidase deficiency = Gaucher disease

wrongOptions.explanation: Krabbe disease presents with developmental regression and peripheral neuropathy but not a cherry-red macula.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Peripheral neuropathy + globoid cells + galactocerebrosidase deficiency = Krabbe disease

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Cherry-red spot + hyperacusis + no hepatomegaly = Tay-Sachs disease

stem: A child is diagnosed with Tay-Sachs disease. Which of the following best describes the underlying pathophysiology?
explanation: Tay-Sachs disease occurs due to deficiency of hexosaminidase A, resulting in accumulation of GM2 gangliosides within neurons and progressive neurodegeneration.
correctAnswerText: A. Accumulation of GM2 ganglioside due to hexosaminidase A deficiency

choices.text: Accumulation of GM2 ganglioside due to hexosaminidase A deficiency
Accumulation of sphingomyelin due to sphingomyelinase deficiency
Accumulation of glucocerebroside due to glucocerebrosidase deficiency
Accumulation of galactocerebroside due to galactocerebrosidase deficiency

wrongOptions.text: B. Accumulation of sphingomyelin due to sphingomyelinase deficiency
wrongOptions.explanation: This describes Niemann-Pick disease rather than Tay-Sachs disease.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Sphingomyelin accumulation + hepatosplenomegaly + cherry-red spot = Niemann-Pick disease

wrongOptions.explanation: This is the underlying defect in Gaucher disease.

wrongOptions.explanation: This mechanism is seen in Krabbe disease.
