stem: A neonate born at 35 weeks has clenched fists with overlapping fingers (index over middle), rocker-bottom feet, micrognathia, a prominent occiput, and a ventricular septal defect on echocardiogram. The most likely chromosomal diagnosis is:
explanation: Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome): clenched fists with overlapping fingers (index over middle, 5th over 4th), rocker-bottom feet, micrognathia, prominent occiput, ventricular septal defect. Second most common autosomal trisomy in live births. Prognosis very poor: 50% die within the first week, 90% by one year.

wrongOptions.explanation: Down syndrome: upslanting palpebral fissures, flat facial profile, single palmar crease, hypotonia, sandal gap, and complete AVSD, not clenched fists or rocker-bottom feet. Completely different dysmorphic phenotype.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Upslanting palpebral fissures + flat face + single palmar crease + hypotonia + AVSD + sandal gap = Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)

wrongOptions.explanation: Trisomy 13: severe midline defects (holoprosencephaly, cyclopia, midline cleft lip/palate), polydactyly, cutis aplasia of scalp, microphthalmia, coloboma. Entirely different phenotype from the clenched fist/rocker-bottom foot pattern of trisomy 18.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Holoprosencephaly + polydactyly + midline cleft lip + cutis aplasia + microphthalmia = Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome)

wrongOptions.explanation: Turner syndrome: phenotypic females with webbed neck, shield chest, widely spaced nipples, coarctation of aorta, primary amenorrhea, short stature,  recognized in childhood/adolescence, not by clenched fists or rocker-bottom feet in the neonatal period.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Female + webbed neck + shield chest + coarctation + primary amenorrhea = Turner syndrome (45,X)

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Clenched overlapping fingers + rocker-bottom feet + micrognathia + prominent occiput + VSD = Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome)

stem: A 3-year-old boy with trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) presents for a well-child visit. In addition to his known intellectual disability, which of the following associated conditions requires routine screening in ALL children with Down syndrome?
explanation: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is associated with a constellation of systemic conditions requiring active surveillance: (1) Congenital heart defects (~50%), especially atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD/endocardial cushion defect) and VSD; echocardiogram in all newborns; (2) Hypothyroidism (~15–20%) — TSH at birth and annually; (3) Atlantoaxial instability,  cervical radiograph before contact sports participation; (4) Duodenal atresia ('double bubble' sign),  in newborns; (5) Hirschsprung disease; (6) Acute myeloid/lymphoid leukemia (~1%); (7) Obstructive sleep apnea; (8) Hearing and vision impairment. These are testable associations on USMLE Step 1.
topicName: Down Syndrome, Associated Conditions and Screening

choices.text: Hypothyroidism (TSH annually), atlantoaxial instability (cervical spine radiograph), and congenital heart disease (echocardiogram in infancy)
Phenylketonuria (plasma phenylalanine level annually) and galactosemia (galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase)
Neurofibromatosis (skin examination for café-au-lait spots) and tuberous sclerosis (renal ultrasound)
Turner syndrome-associated bicuspid aortic valve screening and lymphedema assessment

wrongOptions.text: 1: B) Phenylketonuria (plasma phenylalanine level annually) and galactosemia (galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase)
wrongOptions.explanation: PKU and galactosemia are autosomal recessive inborn errors of metabolism screened on universal newborn screens, they are not specifically associated with Down syndrome. Down syndrome is a chromosomal aneuploidy, not an enzyme deficiency disorder.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: PKU + galactosemia = autosomal recessive enzyme deficiencies; newborn screen targets; not specifically associated with trisomy 21

wrongOptions.text: 2: C) Neurofibromatosis (skin examination for café-au-lait spots) and tuberous sclerosis (renal ultrasound)
wrongOptions.explanation: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1 gene, chromosome 17) and tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2) are neurocutaneous syndromes with autosomal dominant inheritance,  unrelated to trisomy 21.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: NF1 = café-au-lait + Lisch nodules + neurofibromas + chr 17; TSC = ash leaf + shagreen patch + cortical tubers; neither associated with trisomy 21

wrongOptions.text: 3: D) Turner syndrome-associated bicuspid aortic valve screening and lymphedema assessment
wrongOptions.explanation: Turner syndrome (45,X) is associated with bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation of the aorta, lymphedema (webbed neck, cystic hygroma), and primary ovarian insufficiency. These are not features of Down syndrome (trisomy 21)
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Turner (45,X) = bicuspid AoV + coarctation + webbed neck + lymphedema + primary ovarian insufficiency; not features of trisomy 21

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Trisomy 21 associations: AVSD + hypothyroidism + atlantoaxial instability + duodenal atresia + AML/ALL + OSA + hearing/vision loss
tags: Down Syndrome, Associated Conditions and Screening

stem: A 14-year-old boy has tall stature, long fingers, and lens dislocation. His plasma homocysteine is markedly elevated and he has mild intellectual disability. His 11-year-old sister has the same lens dislocation. Both parents are phenotypically normal. The direction of lens dislocation and inheritance pattern are:
explanation: Homocystinuria (CBS deficiency): marfanoid habitus + INFERONASAL/DOWNWARD lens dislocation (opposite of Marfan's upward) + intellectual disability + thromboembolism + elevated homocysteine. Autosomal recessive— both parents unaffected carriers explains two affected children from phenotypically normal parents. CBS mutations: cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency → homocysteine accumulation → connective tissue and CNS effects.
topicName: Marfan vs Homocystinuria,  Lens Direction and Inheritance

wrongOptions.explanation: Superotemporal (upward) ectopia lentis + AD + normal intelligence + FBN1 = Marfan syndrome. This family has two affected children from unaffected parents (AR pattern) + elevated homocysteine — consistent with homocystinuria, not Marfan.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: UPWARD (superotemporal) ectopia lentis + normal intelligence + AD + FBN1 mutation = Marfan syndrome

wrongOptions.explanation: Lens direction (downward) is correct for homocystinuria, but inheritance is AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE. Two affected siblings from two unaffected parents = classic AR pattern (each parent carries one mutated CBS allele, 25% risk per child). AD would require at least one affected parent.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Two affected siblings + two phenotypically normal parents = Autosomal recessive (carrier × carrier → 25% affected per child)

wrongOptions.explanation: Neither feature applies. X-linked recessive primarily affects males with carrier females,  but here a male and female sibling are both affected from unaffected parents (inconsistent with X-linked recessive). Lens dislocation in homocystinuria is downward, not upward.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Males primarily affected + carrier mother + no father-to-son = X-linked recessive (incompatible with affected female sibling)

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Marfanoid + DOWNWARD ectopia lentis + intellectual disability + elevated homocysteine + unaffected carrier parents + AR = Homocystinuria (CBS deficiency)
tags: Marfan vs Homocystinuria,  Lens Direction and Inheritance

stem: A 22-year-old man with Marfan syndrome is found to have an aortic root diameter of 4.7 cm (upper limit of normal 4.0 cm) on echocardiogram. He is asymptomatic. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
explanation: Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation → deficient fibrillin-1 → impaired TGF-β sequestration → aortic medial degeneration) causes progressive aortic root dilation leading to aortic regurgitation and life-threatening aortic dissection (most common cause of death). Management of dilated aortic root: (1) Beta-blockers (reduce dP/dt, aortic wall stress), first-line; losartan (ARB) is an alternative/adjunct via TGF-β pathway; (2) Activity restriction, avoid contact sports, isometric exercise, Valsalva; (3) Prophylactic aortic root replacement is indicated when diameter reaches ~4.5–5.0 cm (guidelines vary) or when growth rate exceeds 0.5 cm/year. At 4.7 cm this patient meets surgical referral threshold.
topicName: Marfan Syndrome, Cardiovascular Complications and Management

choices.text: Start beta-blocker therapy to reduce aortic wall stress and refer for cardiothoracic surgery evaluation for prophylactic aortic root replacement
Reassure the patient that aortic dilation is expected in Marfan syndrome and recheck echocardiogram in 5 years
Start high-intensity exercise training to improve cardiovascular conditioning
Perform emergent aortic dissection repair because the aortic root exceeds 4.0 cm

wrongOptions.text: 1: B) Reassure the patient that aortic dilation is expected in Marfan syndrome and recheck echocardiogram in 5 years
wrongOptions.explanation: While aortic dilation is expected in Marfan syndrome, it is not benign and requires active management. Aortic root dilation above 4.0 cm requires beta-blocker therapy, annual echocardiography (not 5-year intervals), activity restriction, and surgical referral as the diameter approaches operative threshold. Reassurance without intervention at 4.7 cm would be negligent.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Aortic root >4.0 cm = active management required; annual echo + beta-blocker + surgical referral near threshold; 5-year interval insufficient

wrongOptions.text: C) Start high-intensity exercise training to improve cardiovascular conditioning
wrongOptions.explanation: Patients with Marfan syndrome should AVOID strenuous exercise, particularly isometric exercise, contact sports, and activities causing Valsalva maneuver. These raise aortic wall stress and accelerate dilation risk. Competitive athletics are contraindicated once significant aortic root dilation is present.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Marfan + aortic dilation = AVOID isometric exercise, contact sports, Valsalva; high-intensity exercise contraindicated

wrongOptions.text: 3: D) Perform emergent aortic dissection repair because the aortic root exceeds 4.0 cm
wrongOptions.explanation: This patient is asymptomatic with dilation (4.7 cm) but no dissection. Emergency surgery is indicated for acute aortic dissection (severe tearing chest/back pain, pulse differentials, widened mediastinum). Prophylactic elective repair is planned when the root approaches 4.5–5.0 cm; emergent repair is not indicated without dissection.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Aortic dissection = emergent repair; asymptomatic dilation = prophylactic elective repair at 4.5–5.0 cm threshold; not emergent

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Marfan aortic root dilation: beta-blocker to slow progression + surgical referral at ≥4.5–5.0 cm; avoid contact sports/isometric exercise
tags: Marfan Syndrome, Cardiovascular Complications and Management

stem: A bleeding disorder affects all males who inherit the mutation but does not affect carrier females. Affected fathers never transmit the condition to their sons but all their daughters become carriers. The condition appears to skip generations when transmitted through asymptomatic carrier females. This pattern is consistent with:
explanation: X-linked recessive: (1) primarily affects males (hemizygous, one X, one mutant allele sufficient); (2) carrier females unaffected (heterozygous,  second normal X compensates); (3) father-to-son transmission IMPOSSIBLE (fathers give Y to sons, not X); (4) affected fathers → ALL daughters are carriers (receive father's mutant X); (5) appears to skip generations through asymptomatic carrier females. Classic examples: hemophilia A/B, DMD, G6PD deficiency, color blindness.

wrongOptions.explanation: Autosomal dominant: (1) both sexes affected equally; (2) father-to-son transmission IS possible (autosome); (3) every generation typically affected (50% offspring risk). None match the described pattern.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Both sexes affected + father-to-son possible + every generation + 50% offspring risk = Autosomal dominant

wrongOptions.explanation: Autosomal recessive: (1) both sexes affected equally (no sex predilection); (2) both parents typically carriers; (3) horizontal pattern (siblings affected, parents not). The exclusive male involvement and maternal carrier transmission described is inconsistent with AR.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Both sexes affected equally + two unaffected carrier parents + 25% risk per sibling = Autosomal recessive

wrongOptions.explanation: X-linked dominant: both sexes affected (heterozygous females are symptomatic, though often less severely than hemizygous males). The described pattern shows unaffected carrier females — females with the mutation are NOT affected,  specifically indicating X-linked recessive, not dominant.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Both sexes affected (females with one copy still affected, often less severely) + no carrier state = X-linked dominant

buzzwords: daughters of affected fathers all carriers
buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Males affected + carrier females unaffected + no father-to-son + all daughters of affected fathers are carriers = X-linked recessive
tags: daughters of affected fathers all carriers

stem: A 14-year-old boy with slowly progressive proximal muscle weakness has been able to walk independently since age 5. His creatine kinase is 8,200 U/L (markedly elevated). Muscle biopsy shows reduced but present dystrophin. Genetic testing reveals a large in-frame deletion in the DMD gene. Which of the following best explains why his phenotype is milder than classic Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
explanation: The '21-amino acid rule' (Monaco): DMD gene mutations causing out-of-frame (frameshift) deletions disrupt the reading frame, producing a premature stop codon → complete absence of dystrophin → severe Duchenne phenotype (wheelchair by ~12, death by ~20s). In-frame deletions maintain the reading frame → truncated, partially functional dystrophin → milder Becker MD (ambulatory into adulthood, normal lifespan possible). This is the molecular basis distinguishing DMD from BMD. Both are X-linked recessive. Muscle biopsy in DMD: absent dystrophin on immunostaining; in BMD: reduced/abnormal dystrophin.
topicName: Duchenne vs Becker Muscular Dystrophy,  Frameshift vs In-frame Mutation

choices.text: An in-frame deletion preserves the reading frame, producing a truncated but partially functional dystrophin protein (Becker MD); a frameshift deletion in DMD produces a premature stop codon, no functional dystrophin, and a severe phenotype
The in-frame deletion causes complete absence of dystrophin, which paradoxically results in a milder phenotype due to compensatory utrophin upregulation
Becker MD results from a point mutation in the dystrophin gene, while Duchenne results from a deletion
His milder phenotype is explained by X-inactivation protecting one copy of the dystrophin gene

wrongOptions.text: 1: B) The in-frame deletion causes complete absence of dystrophin, which paradoxically results in a milder phenotype due to compensatory utrophin upregulation
wrongOptions.explanation: Complete absence of dystrophin is the hallmark of Duchenne (frameshift mutation), not Becker. While utrophin upregulation is a real therapeutic target being studied for DMD, it does not explain the milder phenotype in this patient. His biopsy shows reduced but present dystrophin, consistent with an in-frame Becker mutation.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Absent dystrophin = DMD (frameshift); reduced/present dystrophin = BMD (in-frame); utrophin upregulation = research target, not explanation for natural Becker phenotype

wrongOptions.text: 2: C) Becker MD results from a point mutation in the dystrophin gene, while Duchenne results from a deletion
wrongOptions.explanation: Both DMD and Becker MD most commonly result from deletions in the dystrophin gene. The critical distinction is not the mutation TYPE (deletion vs point mutation) but the mutation's effect on the reading frame: out-of-frame deletion → DMD; in-frame deletion → BMD. Point mutations can also cause either phenotype depending on their effect on the reading frame.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: DMD vs BMD = frameshift vs in-frame (reading frame effect), NOT deletion vs point mutation

wrongOptions.text: 3: D) His milder phenotype is explained by X-inactivation protecting one copy of the dystrophin gene
wrongOptions.explanation: X-inactivation occurs in females (46,XX),  one X chromosome is inactivated in each cell. This patient is male (46,XY) with only one X chromosome, so X-inactivation does not apply. Female carriers of DMD mutations may have mild symptoms due to skewed X-inactivation, but this mechanism is irrelevant for an affected male.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: X-inactivation = female phenomenon (two X chromosomes); does not apply to affected males with only one X chromosome

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Frameshift deletion = premature stop = absent dystrophin = DMD (severe); In-frame deletion = truncated dystrophin = BMD (mild); same DMD gene
tags: Duchenne vs Becker Muscular Dystrophy,  Frameshift vs In-frame Mutation

stem: A 68-year-old man has intention tremor, gait ataxia, and mild cognitive decline diagnosed as FXTAS. His daughter is an asymptomatic carrier. His 8-year-old grandson has severe intellectual disability, macroorchidism, and autism-like behaviors. The molecular mechanism causing progressively more severe disease in successive generations is:
explanation: Fragile X syndrome demonstrates anticipation via CGG repeat expansion in FMR1: Normal ≤44 repeats; Premutation 55–200 repeats (grandfather with FXTAS,  tremor/ataxia in older males with premutation; female carriers risk premature ovarian insufficiency); Full mutation >200 repeats (grandson: intellectual disability, macroorchidism, autism). Repeats expand during maternal transmission, causing progressively more severe disease = anticipation.
topicName: Trinucleotide Repeat Expansion and Anticipation,  Fragile X

choices.text: CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene — anticipation causes expanding repeats and worsening severity across generations
Variable expressivity of an autosomal dominant point mutation
Genomic imprinting — parent-of-origin determines which allele is expressed
Accumulation of somatic mutations in mitochondrial DNA across generations

wrongOptions.text: 1: B) Variable expressivity of an autosomal dominant mutation
wrongOptions.explanation: Variable expressivity describes unpredictable differences in severity among family members with the same mutation — without directional generational worsening. Fragile X shows predictable , directional worsening due to repeat expansion (anticipation). Also Fragile X is X-linked, not autosomal dominant.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Same mutation + variable severity in family members without directional trend = Variable expressivity (not anticipation)

wrongOptions.explanation: Genomic imprinting = parent-of-origin-specific gene expression. Explains Prader-Willi (paternal 15q11-13 deletion or maternal UPD15) and Angelman syndrome (maternal deletion or paternal UPD15). FMR1 is not imprinted, the worsening across generations in Fragile X is due to CGG repeat expansion (anticipation), not imprinting
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Disease expression depends on which PARENT contributed the chromosome → Genomic imprinting (e.g., Prader-Willi vs Angelman depending on parent of origin)

wrongOptions.explanation: Somatic mutations accumulate within one individual's lifetime but are not heritably transmitted to offspring through germline. The progressive expansion of CGG repeats in FMR1 is a heritable germline  phenomenon,  the expanded repeat is passed in the gamete. This is fundamentally different from somatic mutation accumulation.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Mutations in non-germline cells accumulating during life = Somatic mutations (not heritable to offspring)

buzzwords: grandson severe intellectual disability and macroorchidism
buzzwordCombinationCorrect: CGG repeats expand with each generation through maternal transmission → premutation (FXTAS in males) → full mutation (intellectual disability + macroorchidism + autism) = Fragile X anticipation
tags: Trinucleotide Repeat Expansion and Anticipation,  Fragile X
grandson severe intellectual disability and macroorchidism

stem: An 8-year-old boy presents with recurrent hemarthroses, easy bruising, and prolonged bleeding after dental extraction. His CBC is normal. Labs: PT normal, aPTT prolonged, bleeding time normal, platelet count normal. He is found to have Factor VIII deficiency. His maternal uncle has a similar condition. Which of the following correctly identifies his diagnosis, inheritance pattern, and treatment?
explanation: A) Hemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency); X-linked recessive; treat with recombinant Factor VIII concentrate B) Hemophilia B (Factor IX deficiency); X-linked recessive; treat with recombinant Factor IX concentrate C) Von Willebrand disease; autosomal dominant; treat with DDAVP (desmopressin) D) Hemophilia A; autosomal recessive; treat with fresh frozen plasma
topicName: Hemophilia A vs B, Factor Deficiency and Treatment

choices.text: Hemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency); X-linked recessive; treat with recombinant Factor VIII concentrate
Hemophilia B (Factor IX deficiency); X-linked recessive; treat with recombinant Factor IX concentrate
Von Willebrand disease; autosomal dominant; treat with DDAVP (desmopressin)
Hemophilia A; autosomal recessive; treat with fresh frozen plasma

wrongOptions.text: 1: B) Hemophilia B (Factor IX deficiency); X-linked recessive; treat with recombinant Factor IX concentrate
wrongOptions.explanation: Hemophilia B (Christmas disease) has an identical clinical presentation to Hemophilia A (hemarthroses, prolonged aPTT, normal PT, X-linked recessive) but results from Factor IX deficiency. The specific factor assay showing Factor VIII deficiency distinguishes them. Treatment for B is Factor IX, not Factor VIII.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Hemophilia B = Factor IX deficiency; identical presentation to A; distinguished by factor assay; treat with recombinant Factor IX

wrongOptions.text: 2: C) Von Willebrand disease; autosomal dominant; treat with DDAVP (desmopressin)
wrongOptions.explanation: Von Willebrand disease (vWD) presents with mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, menorrhagia, gum bleeding) and a prolonged bleeding time (platelet plug formation depends on vWF). The aPTT may be mildly elevated because vWF stabilizes Factor VIII. However, hemarthroses are not typical of vWD,  they indicate deep coagulation pathway defects (hemophilia). The normal bleeding time in this patient argues against vWD.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: vWD = mucocutaneous bleeding + prolonged bleeding time + vWF deficiency; hemarthroses = hemophilia not vWD

wrongOptions.text: 3: D) Hemophilia A; autosomal recessive; treat with fresh frozen plasma
wrongOptions.explanation: Hemophilia A is X-linked recessive, not autosomal recessive. The affected maternal uncle pattern confirms X-linked inheritance. Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) contains all clotting factors but is non-specific, requires large volumes, and carries infection risk,  recombinant factor concentrates are the preferred targeted treatment.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Hemophilia A = X-linked recessive (not autosomal recessive); treat with recombinant Factor VIII (not FFP)

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Hemophilia A = Factor VIII; X-linked recessive; hemarthroses + prolonged aPTT + normal PT/BT; treatment = recombinant Factor VIII; maternal uncle = X-linked pattern
tags: Hemophilia A vs B, Factor Deficiency and Treatment

stem: A senior resident is on overnight call when she admits her third patient this week with pulmonary embolism. The following morning, a 44-year-old woman presents with pleuritic chest pain, mild dyspnea, and a heart rate of 102 bpm. The resident orders a CT pulmonary angiogram immediately, before completing a full history, without calculating a pre-test probability score. The history later reveals the patient recently returned from a 14-hour international flight and has no other risk factors for PE; however, the CT scan is negative and the patient is diagnosed with musculoskeletal chest pain. The cognitive error that most directly led to the immediate CT order is:
explanation: The availability heuristic is a mental shortcut in which the probability of an event is estimated based on how easily similar examples come to mind. Because the resident had recently admitted three PE patients, making PE cognitively 'available',  she overestimated the pre-test probability of PE in this patient and bypassed structured pre-test probability scoring (e.g., Wells criteria). The clinical data actually supported a low pre-test probability: young woman, single risk factor (recent long-haul flight), pleuritic pain that could be musculoskeletal. Availability bias is specifically triggered by the salience of recent, vivid, or repeated experiences,  exactly the three recent PE admissions.
topicName: Availability Heuristic / Cognitive Bias in Clinical Decision-Making
system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills

choices.text: Availability heuristic — recent repeated exposure to PE cases inflated the perceived probability of PE beyond what the clinical data justified
Anchoring bias — the resident anchored to tachycardia as the primary diagnostic clue and failed to consider musculoskeletal causes
Premature closure — the resident stopped the diagnostic workup once CT-PE was negative and did not pursue further investigation
Overdiagnosis bias — the resident knowingly over-tested to avoid medicolegal risk, not due to cognitive error

wrongOptions.explanation: Anchoring requires a pre-formed initial diagnosis that is not revised. Here the resident did not anchor to a prior label, she formed her PE suspicion rapidly based on recent experience, not a documented prior impression. The error is about the source of probability estimation, not the failure to revise.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Prior label in chart + discordant new findings + unchanged management = Anchoring bias

wrongOptions.explanation: Premature closure describes stopping the diagnostic process after reaching a diagnosis. The resident did not stop after a diagnosis, she stopped before one (no pre-test probability was calculated) and the imaging was negative. The error occurred at the initiation of the workup, not at its termination.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Diagnosis accepted without considering alternatives + workup terminated early = Premature closure

wrongOptions.explanation: Overdiagnosis bias is not a standard cognitive heuristic in behavioral science. The resident's decision was driven by cognitive availability, not calculated risk-aversion or medicolegal strategy.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Conscious decision to over-test for liability purposes = Defensive medicine (not a cognitive bias)

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Recent repeated similar diagnosis + overestimated probability + bypassed pre-test scoring = Availability heuristic
tags: Availability Heuristic / Cognitive Bias in Clinical Decision-Making
Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills

stem: A 38-year-old accountant with recently diagnosed rheumatoid arthritis tells her primary care physician that she has taken a leave of absence from work, is excused from her household responsibilities by her spouse, expects her physician to 'fix her completely,' and believes she has no obligation to adhere to her prescribed methotrexate regimen because 'that's the doctor's job, not mine.' According to Talcott Parsons' sociological model of illness, which of the following rights and obligations is this patient incorrectly applying?
explanation: Talcott Parsons (1951) described the sick role as a sociological construct with two rights and two obligations. The two rights are: (1) exemption from normal social role responsibilities (work, household duties), proportional to the severity of illness; and (2) not being held morally responsible for the illness (sickness is involuntary). The two obligations are: (1) the sick person must want to get well and work toward recovery, illness is not a desirable permanent state; and (2) the sick person must seek technically competent medical help and comply with treatment. This patient correctly exercises her rights: she takes leave (right 1) and is not blamed for having RA (right 2). However, she violates both obligations: she refuses to see medication adherence as her responsibility (obligation 2 violated) and implicitly suggests her recovery is entirely the physician's domain (obligation 1 undermined). The answer identifies the specific violation: exemption is correctly applied, but the obligation to cooperate with treatment is not.
topicName: Sick Role (Parsons' Sociological Model) / Illness Behavior
system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills

choices.text: The patient is correctly exempt from normal role obligations but incorrectly believes she has no obligation to cooperate with treatment and seek competent medical care
The patient is correctly exempt from work obligations but incorrectly retains the right to be considered morally responsible for her illness
The patient incorrectly claims exemption from work because Parsons' model only applies to acute, not chronic, illness
The patient is exercising all four components of the sick role correctly; her refusal of medication is protected under patient autonomy rights

wrongOptions.text: 1: B) Correctly exempt from work but incorrectly retains moral responsibility
wrongOptions.explanation: Parsons' sick role explicitly exempts the ill person from moral responsibility for their illness, being sick is considered an involuntary state. This patient is NOT incorrectly claiming moral responsibility; she never does so. The answer conflates the rights with the obligations and misidentifies which component is violated.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Sick person blamed for illness + moral culpability assigned = Violation of sick role right 2 (moral exemption)

wrongOptions.text: 2: C) Exemption only applies to acute illness
wrongOptions.explanation: Parsons' original model was critiqued for applying most cleanly to acute illness, but the model itself does not restrict sick role rights to acute conditions. In practice, chronic illness patients may exercise modified versions of sick role rights. The work exemption for RA (a disabling autoimmune condition) is clinically and sociologically appropriate and is not the error being identified.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Chronic illness + sick role exemption disputed = Critique of Parsons' model (not a patient violation)

wrongOptions.text: 3: D) Patient is exercising all four components correctly
wrongOptions.explanation: This is clearly incorrect. Patient autonomy does not include the right to refuse one's own treatment obligations under the sick role. While patients may refuse treatment legally, Parsons' sociological model specifically identifies cooperation with treatment as an obligation of the sick role. The patient who demands the rights without fulfilling the obligations is misapplying the model.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Rights exercised + obligations refused + patient autonomy invoked = Misapplication of sick role obligations

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Exempt from normal duties (RIGHT) + not morally blamed (RIGHT) + must seek to recover (OBLIGATION violated) + must comply with treatment (OBLIGATION violated) = Sick Role, Parsons
tags: Sick Role (Parsons' Sociological Model) / Illness Behavior
Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
Adherence and compliance in chronic disease

stem: A patient with acute kidney injury several weeks after coronary angiography undergoes a skin biopsy. Microscopic examination reveals needle-shaped empty spaces within small arteries surrounded by an inflammatory infiltrate. This finding is most consistent with:
explanation: Needle-shaped empty spaces (cholesterol clefts) within small arteries are pathognomonic for cholesterol embolization syndrome. The clefts represent the spaces left behind when cholesterol crystals are dissolved during tissue processing.
correctAnswerText: A) Cholesterol clefts in small arteries

choices.text: Apple-green birefringence with Congo red staining

wrongOptions.explanation: Seen in malignant hypertension and polyarteritis nodosa — bright pink glassy necrotic arteriolar walls, not needle-shaped empty clefts.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Malignant HTN / PAN + bright pink glassy arteriolar necrosis = fibrinoid necrosis

wrongOptions.text: C) Apple-green birefringence with Congo red staining
wrongOptions.explanation: The hallmark of amyloidosis from extracellular amyloid deposition, not cholesterol embolization.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Congo red + apple-green birefringence = amyloidosis

wrongOptions.explanation: Characteristic of ANCA-associated vasculitis (GPA, MPA, EGPA) on renal biopsy.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Pauci-immune crescents + positive ANCA = ANCA-associated vasculitis

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Post-vascular procedure + needle-shaped empty spaces in small arteries = cholesterol clefts (cholesterol embolization syndrome)

stem: An elderly patient develops painful, dusky blue toes with intact distal pulses 2 weeks after cardiac catheterization. Which of the following best explains this finding?
explanation: "Blue toe syndrome" — digital ischemia with intact distal pulses — reflects microvascular occlusion by cholesterol crystals embolizing from an atherosclerotic plaque. Distal pulses are preserved because the larger feeding arteries remain patent; only the small arteries supplying the digits are occluded.
topicName: Cholesterol embolization syndrome — blue toe syndrome
correctAnswerText: A) Microvascular occlusion by cholesterol crystals embolizing from atherosclerotic plaque

choices.text: Microvascular occlusion by cholesterol crystals embolizing from atherosclerotic plaque
Occlusive thrombus in a major peripheral artery
Vasospasm of digital arteries from cold exposure

wrongOptions.text: B) Occlusive thrombus in a major peripheral artery
wrongOptions.explanation: Large-artery thrombotic occlusion produces absent distal pulses (acute limb ischemia with the 6 P's), not blue toes with intact pulses.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Acute limb ischemia + absent pulses + 6 P's = large-vessel arterial occlusion

wrongOptions.text: C) Vasospasm of digital arteries from cold exposure
wrongOptions.explanation: Describes Raynaud phenomenon — triphasic color changes (white → blue → red) on cold exposure with normal warm baseline, not persistent blue toes after a vascular procedure.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Cold-induced triphasic color change (white-blue-red) = Raynaud phenomenon

wrongOptions.text: D) Systemic vasculitis with palpable purpura
wrongOptions.explanation: Vasculitis (e.g., hypersensitivity, IgA, ANCA-associated) produces palpable purpura rather than blue toes with intact pulses, and has different inciting factors.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Palpable purpura + leukocytoclastic vasculitis on biopsy = hypersensitivity vasculitis

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Post-catheterization + blue toes + intact distal pulses = cholesterol microemboli (blue toe syndrome)
tags: Cholesterol embolization syndrome — blue toe syndrome

stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of chronic kidney disease is evaluated during a routine follow-up. Laboratory studies show a serum creatinine of 4.0 mg/dL. The physician estimates the patient's glomerular filtration rate (GFR) using a 24-hour urine creatinine clearance test. The calculated creatinine clearance is determined to be 30 mL/min. However, the true GFR measured via inulin clearance is actually 24 mL/min. Which of the following transport mechanisms best explains why the calculated clearance of creatinine overestimates the true GFR in this patient?
explanation: Creatinine is freely filtered at the glomerulus, but it is also moderately secreted by the proximal renal tubules via organic anion/cation transporters. Because the total excreted amount in urine includes both the filtered load and the secreted amount (Ucr ×V increases), the mathematical calculation for clearance ( UCr × V /Pcr ) slightly overestimates the true GFR.
topicName: Acute Kidney Injury / Glomerular Filtration Rate Reduction

choices.text: Passive reabsorption in the collecting duct
Carrier-mediated secretion in the proximal tubule
Facilitated diffusion in the thick ascending limb
Paracellular reabsorption in the distal tubule

wrongOptions.text: A) Passive reabsorption in the collecting duct
wrongOptions.explanation: If a substance undergoes significant reabsorption, its renal clearance value would drop below the true GFR. Urea exhibits this behavior, but creatinine does not undergo passive reabsorption along the collecting duct.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Serum creatinine + Clearance lower than GFR = Passive reabsorption in the collecting duct

wrongOptions.text: C) Facilitated diffusion in the thick ascending limb
wrongOptions.explanation: The thick ascending limb is highly involved in active ion transport (Na+/K +/2Cl− ) and is impermeable to water, but it plays no role in the active secretion or modification of creatinine levels.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Chronic kidney disease + Medullary concentration gradient = Facilitated diffusion in the thick ascending limb

wrongOptions.text: D) Paracellular reabsorption in the distal tubule
wrongOptions.explanation: Paracellular reabsorption in the distal segments handles ions like calcium and magnesium under hormonal control. This choice is wrong as the specific physiology of creatinine overestimation is confined strictly to active secretion.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Electrolyte handling + Distal nephron segment = Paracellular reabsorption in the distal tubule

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Creatinine clearance + Overestimates true GFR + Proximal renal tubules = Carrier-mediated secretion in the proximal tubule
tags: Acute Kidney Injury / Glomerular Filtration Rate Reduction

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his mother because of progressive swelling around his eyes and ankles over the past week. Urinalysis reveals 4+ proteinuria, but no hematuria or casts. The primary defect in this patient's condition involves a barrier that limits the filtration of molecules based on both size and charge. Which of the following components of this barrier is primarily responsible for preventing the filtration of negatively charged proteins like albumin?
explanation: The glomerular filtration barrier utilizes a charge barrier composed of negatively charged glycoproteins (such as heparan sulfate) within the glomerular basement membrane and endothelial surface to repel like-charged molecules. Since albumin is negatively charged, this electrostatic repulsion prevents its filtration into Bowman's space. Effacement of podocyte foot processes disrupts this architecture, leading to massive selective proteinuria.

wrongOptions.explanation: The fenestrated capillary endothelium acts primarily as a size barrier that prevents the entry of large molecules and cellular elements (> 100 nm) into the wall. It does not provide the primary negative charge repulsion that selectively halts albumin.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Swelling around eyes + 4+ proteinuria + Size barrier = Fenestrated capillary endothelium

wrongOptions.explanation: The slit diaphragms between podocyte foot processes function primarily as a physical size barrier preventing the entry of molecules larger than 40–50 nm.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Effacement of podocyte foot processes + Size barrier = Podocyte slit diaphragms

wrongOptions.text: D) Proximal convoluted tubule brush border
wrongOptions.explanation: The proximal convoluted tubule brush border is responsible for macromolecule reabsorption via endocytosis, not the initial filtration barrier filtration screening. It does not establish the charge barrier of the glomerulus.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Proteinuria + Macromolecule reabsorption = Proximal convoluted tubule brush border

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: 4+ proteinuria + Effacement of podocyte foot processes + Charge barrier = Glomerular basement membrane polyanions

stem: A male infant develops urinary retention and bilateral hydronephrosis shortly after birth due to bladder outlet obstruction. Which of the following congenital urinary tract abnormalities is the most likely cause?
explanation: Posterior urethral valves are obstructing membranous folds within the posterior urethra that cause bladder outlet obstruction in male infants. Severe obstruction may lead to urinary retention, bilateral hydronephrosis, oligohydramnios, and progressive renal damage

wrongOptions.explanation: Vesicoureteral reflux results from incompetence of the ureterovesical junction and commonly presents with recurrent urinary tract infections and renal scarring. The disorder causes retrograde urine flow rather than direct bladder outlet obstruction.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Recurrent childhood UTIs + retrograde urine flow + renal scarring = Vesicoureteral reflux

wrongOptions.explanation: Horseshoe kidney results from fusion of the lower poles of the kidneys and failure of normal ascent due to entrapment beneath the inferior mesenteric artery. Many patients are asymptomatic, although urinary obstruction and infections may occur.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Fused lower poles + Turner Syndrome = Horseshoe kidney

wrongOptions.explanation: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction causes hydronephrosis due to impaired urine drainage from the renal pelvis into the ureter. It typically produces unilateral hydronephrosis rather than bladder outlet obstruction.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Hydronephrosis + impaired  drainage + UPJ narrowing = UPJ obstruction

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Male infant + bladder outlet obstruction + bilateral hydronephrosis = Posterior urethral valves

stem: A fetus develops severe bilateral hydronephrosis due to bladder outlet obstruction from posterior urethral valves. Which of the following fetal complications is most strongly associated with this condition?
explanation: Posterior urethral valves can cause severe fetal urinary tract obstruction leading to oligohydramnios due to decreased fetal urine output. Reduced amniotic fluid impairs normal lung development and may result in pulmonary hypoplasia as part of Potter sequence
correctAnswerText: B) Pulmonary hypoplasia due to oligohydramnios

choices.text: Neural tube defects due to folate deficiency
Meconium ileus due to pancreatic insufficiency

wrongOptions.explanation: Polyhydramnios commonly occurs in conditions that impair fetal swallowing, such as esophageal atresia or anencephaly, rather than urinary tract obstruction. Excess amniotic fluid accumulates because swallowed fluid cannot be properly absorbed
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Impaired swallowing + excess fluid + esophageal atresia = Polyhydramnios

wrongOptions.text: Neural tube defects due to folate deficiency
wrongOptions.explanation: Neural tube defects result from failure of neural tube closure during embryogenesis and are associated with folate deficiency. Common examples include spina bifida and anencephaly
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Folate deficiency + failed neural tube closure = Neural tube defects

wrongOptions.text: Meconium ileus due to pancreatic insufficiency
wrongOptions.explanation: Cystic fibrosis is associated with meconium ileus due to thick abnormal secretions causing neonatal intestinal obstruction. Patients also commonly develop pancreatic insufficiency and recurrent pulmonary infections
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Pancreatic insufficiency + meconium ileus + CFTR mutation = Cystic fibrosis

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: urinary obstruction + oligohydramnios + pulmonary hypoplasia = Potter sequence

stem: Which of the following vascular findings is most characteristic of malignant hypertension affecting the kidneys?
explanation: Malignant hypertension causes severe vascular injury leading to hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis characterized by concentric “onion-skin” thickening of arteriolar walls. Fibrinoid necrosis may also occur in affected vessels

choices.text: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis with gradual luminal narrowing
Thickened glomerular basement membrane with spike-and-dome appearance

wrongOptions.text: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis with gradual luminal narrowing
wrongOptions.explanation: Benign nephrosclerosis is caused by long-standing hypertension leading to hyaline thickening of small renal arterioles and chronic renal ischemia. The process develops gradually and is associated with slowly progressive renal dysfunction.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Chronic hypertension + hyaline arterioles +Chronic  renal ischemia = Benign nephrosclerosis

wrongOptions.explanation: Diabetic nephropathy is characterized by Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules due to chronic hyperglycemia and nonenzymatic glycosylation injury. Patients commonly develop proteinuria and progressive chronic kidney disease.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Diabetes mellitus + Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules + Proteinuria= Diabetic nephropathy

wrongOptions.text: Thickened glomerular basement membrane with spike-and-dome appearance
wrongOptions.explanation: Membranous nephropathy demonstrates subepithelial immune complex deposition producing a characteristic spike-and-dome appearance. It is a common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adult
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Spike-and-dome deposits + subepithelial immune complexes + nephrotic syndrome = Membranous nephropathy

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Severe hypertension + onion-skin arterioles + fibrinoid necrosis = Malignant hypertension

stem: A 52-year-old man with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension and diabetes mellitus undergoes routine follow-up. Physical examination is unremarkable, and serum creatinine is normal. Which of the following findings is most suggestive of early diabetic nephropathy?
explanation: Diabetic nephropathy initially presents with microalbuminuria due to early glomerular damage from chronic hyperglycemia. Persistent microalbuminuria is an important early marker of diabetic kidney disease and may progress to nephrotic-range proteinuria over time.

choices.text: Massive hematuria with red blood cell casts

wrongOptions.text: Massive hematuria with red blood cell casts
wrongOptions.explanation: Glomerulonephritis is characterized by red blood cell casts and significant hematuria due to glomerular inflammation. These findings are more consistent with nephritic syndromes than early diabetic nephropathy
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: RBC casts + glomerular inflammation + nephritic syndrome = Glomerulonephritis

wrongOptions.explanation: Immune complex glomerulonephritis commonly produces low complement levels due to immune complex activation of the complement cascade. Examples include poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis and lupus nephritis.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Immune complex deposition + complement consumption +RBC cast= Lupus nephritis

wrongOptions.explanation: Multiple myeloma is associated with Bence Jones proteins, which are monoclonal light chains filtered into the urine. Patients may also develop lytic bone lesions, hypercalcemia, and renal failure.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Monoclonal light chains + plasma cell proliferation + Bence Jones proteinuria = Multiple myeloma

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Diabetes mellitus + early glomerular injury + microalbuminuria = Diabetic nephropathy

stem:
67-year-old man with stable angina develops sudden chest discomfort while climbing stairs. In the emergency department, he is given a medication that increases nitric oxide signaling, leading to relaxation of vascular smooth muscle and rapid vasodilation. A medical student asks how smooth muscle relaxation occurs at the molecular level. The attending physician explains that nitric oxide increases intracellular levels of a second messenger that activates myosin light-chain phosphatase (MLCP), promoting smooth muscle relaxation.
Which of the following substances most directly activates myosin light-chain phosphatase (MLCP) in this patient?
explanation: Nitric oxide stimulates guanylate cyclase, increasing intracellular cGMP levels. cGMP activates myosin light-chain phosphatase (MLCP), which dephosphorylates myosin light chains and promotes smooth muscle relaxation.

wrongOptions.explanation: cAMP can promote smooth muscle relaxation in some tissues, but nitric oxide-mediated activation of MLCP occurs primarily through cGMP signaling.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: β-adrenergic signaling + protein kinase A + bronchodilation = cAMP

wrongOptions.explanation: Increased intracellular calcium promotes smooth muscle contraction by activating the calmodulin–MLCK pathway.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Ca2+–calmodulin + myosin phosphorylation + contraction = MLCK activation

wrongOptions.explanation: Troponin C is involved in skeletal and cardiac muscle contraction, not smooth muscle regulation.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Troponin + thin filament regulation + striated muscle = skeletal/cardiac muscle contraction

buzzwords: substances most directly activates myosin light-chain phosphatase
buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Nitric oxide + smooth muscle relaxation + MLCP activation = cGMP
tags: substances most directly activates myosin light-chain phosphatase

stem: A patient is brought to the emergency department after a pelvic fracture from a motor vehicle collision. He is unable to urinate and has gross hematuria. Which of the following physical examination findings most strongly suggests posterior urethral injury?
explanation: Posterior urethral injury commonly occurs after pelvic fractures and may cause urethral disruption with displacement of the prostate superiorly, producing a “high-riding” prostate on rectal examination. Patients often present with inability to void and gross hematuria
correctAnswerText: A) High-riding prostate on rectal examination

wrongOptions.explanation: Costovertebral angle tenderness is more suggestive of renal pathology such as pyelonephritis or renal trauma rather than urethral disruption. It reflects inflammation or injury involving the kidneys.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Flank tenderness + renal inflammation + pyelonephritis = Costovertebral Angle tenderness

wrongOptions.explanation: Perineal ecchymosis may occur after pelvic trauma and can suggest underlying genitourinary injury. However, it is less specific for posterior urethral disruption than a high-riding prostate.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Pelvic trauma + Perineal ecchymosis + soft tissue injury = Urethral Injury

wrongOptions.explanation: Suprapubic fullness may occur in bladder outlet obstruction or urinary retention and can also be seen in bladder injury. It is less specific for posterior urethral disruption than a high-riding prostate
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Urinary retention + suprapubic distention= Geinatourinary injury

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Pelvic fracture + high-riding prostate + inability to void = Posterior urethral injury

stem:
61-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease presents to the emergency department with crushing substernal chest pain. He is given sublingual nitroglycerin, and within minutes his chest pain improves due to relaxation of vascular smooth muscle and dilation of coronary vessels. A medical student asks how nitric oxide produces smooth muscle relaxation at the intracellular level.
The attending physician explains that nitric oxide diffuses into smooth muscle cells and activates an enzyme that converts guanosine triphosphate (GTP) into cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), leading to vasodilation.
Which of the following enzymes is most directly responsible for the conversion of GTP to cGMP in smooth muscle cells?
explanation: Nitric oxide activates soluble guanylate cyclase within smooth muscle cells. Guanylate cyclase converts GTP into cGMP, which subsequently activates pathways leading to smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation.

wrongOptions.explanation: Adenylate cyclase converts ATP into cAMP, not GTP into cGMP.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: ATP → cAMP + G protein signaling + β-adrenergic pathway = adenylate cyclase

wrongOptions.explanation: MLCK promotes smooth muscle contraction by phosphorylating myosin light chains.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Ca2+–calmodulin + myosin phosphorylation + contraction = MLCK

wrongOptions.explanation: PDE-5 breaks down cGMP and terminates smooth muscle relaxation signaling.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: cGMP degradation + sildenafil target + erectile physiology = PDE-5

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Nitric oxide + GTP → cGMP + smooth muscle relaxation = guanylate cyclase

stem: Which portion of the bladder is most likely to rupture during blunt trauma to a distended bladder?
explanation: Intraperitoneal bladder rupture most commonly occurs at the bladder dome because it is the weakest and most distensible portion of the bladder. Blunt trauma to a distended bladder may cause rupture with leakage of urine into the peritoneal cavity.

wrongOptions.explanation: The trigone is a relatively fixed and structurally supported region of the bladder located between the ureteral openings and urethra.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Fixed bladder base + ureteral openings = Trigone

wrongOptions.explanation: The bladder neck is associated with the internal urethral sphincter and outlet of the bladder rather than the most common site of rupture during blunt trauma.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Internal sphincter region + bladder outlet = Bladder neck

wrongOptions.explanation: The ureterovesical junction functions as a valve preventing reflux of urine from the bladder into the ureters.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Anti-reflux mechanism + ureter insertion = Ureterovesical junction

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Distended bladder + blunt trauma + dome rupture = Intraperitoneal bladder injury

stem:
A 21-year-old athlete visits a sports medicine clinic after experiencing repeated episodes of muscle tightness during sprint training. During the neurologic examination, the physician taps the patient’s patellar tendon, causing immediate contraction of the quadriceps muscle along with relaxation of the hamstring muscles. A medical student asks how activation of muscle stretch receptors produces both contraction of the agonist muscle and inhibition of the antagonist muscle during the stretch reflex.
The physician explains that sensory fibers from muscle spindles enter the spinal cord and produce two simultaneous effects that coordinate the reflex response.
Which of the following spinal cord events is most directly responsible for this coordinated reflex action?
explanation: Muscle spindle Ia afferent fibers mediate the stretch reflex by directly activating α motor neurons supplying the stretched muscle while simultaneously activating inhibitory interneurons that suppress α motor neurons to the antagonist muscle. This coordinated mechanism produces contraction of the agonist muscle and relaxation of the antagonist muscle (reciprocal inhibition).
correctAnswerText: A. Activation of inhibitory interneurons and α motor neurons

choices.text: Activation of inhibitory interneurons and α motor neurons
Activation of Golgi tendon organ Ib fibers
Inhibition of muscle spindle afferent fibers

wrongOptions.text: B. Activation of Golgi tendon organ Ib fibers
wrongOptions.explanation: Golgi tendon organs respond to excessive muscle tension rather than sudden muscle stretch.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Muscle tension + tendon receptor + autogenic inhibition = Golgi tendon organ

wrongOptions.text: C. Inhibition of muscle spindle afferent fibers
wrongOptions.explanation: Muscle spindle afferents are activated, not inhibited, during the stretch reflex.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Decreased spindle firing + reduced stretch signaling ≠ stretch reflex

wrongOptions.text: D. Activation of postganglionic sympathetic neurons
wrongOptions.explanation: Sympathetic fibers regulate smooth muscle and glandular activity, not skeletal muscle stretch reflexes.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Autonomic output + smooth muscle innervation = sympathetic nervous system

buzzwords: physician taps the patient’s patellar tendon
causing immediate contraction of the quadriceps muscle along with relaxation of the hamstring muscles
buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Muscle stretch reflex + reciprocal inhibition + agonist contraction = activation of inhibitory interneurons and α motor neurons
tags: physician taps the patient’s patellar tendon
causing immediate contraction of the quadriceps muscle along with relaxation of the hamstring muscles

stem:
A 32-year-old man visits a neurology clinic because of progressive numbness in his feet and difficulty maintaining balance. During the physical examination, the physician tests the patient’s patellar reflex by tapping the patellar tendon with a reflex hammer. The quadriceps muscle rapidly contracts, producing extension of the leg. A medical student asks which specialized sensory receptor detects sudden muscle stretch and initiates this reflex response.
The physician explains that a specific proprioceptive receptor located within skeletal muscle is primarily responsible for mediating deep tendon reflexes.
Which of the following structures is most responsible for deep tendon reflexes?
explanation: Muscle spindles are stretch-sensitive proprioceptors located within skeletal muscle. They detect rapid muscle stretch and initiate deep tendon reflexes through Ia afferent fibers that synapse directly with α motor neurons in the spinal cord.

wrongOptions.explanation: Golgi tendon organs detect muscle tension rather than muscle stretch.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Muscle tension + tendon receptor + autogenic inhibition = Golgi tendon organ

wrongOptions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles detect vibration and deep pressure
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Vibration sensation + rapidly adapting receptor = Pacinian corpuscle

wrongOptions.explanation: Free nerve endings primarily detect pain and temperature.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Pain sensation + temperature detection = free nerve ending

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Muscle stretch + patellar reflex + proprioceptor = muscle spindle

stem: In a child with tetralogy of Fallot, which of the following factors most directly determines the severity of cyanosis?
explanation: The degree of pulmonary stenosis is the key determinant of cyanosis severity in tetralogy of Fallot. More severe RV outflow obstruction raises RV pressure above LV pressure, increasing the right-to-left shunt across the VSD and driving more deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation.
correctAnswerText: A) The degree of pulmonary (right ventricular outflow) stenosis

choices.text: The degree of pulmonary (right ventricular outflow) stenosis
The size of the ventricular septal defect
The extent of right ventricular hypertrophy

wrongOptions.text: B) The size of the ventricular septal defect
wrongOptions.explanation: The VSD is typically large and non-restrictive in TOF, so it does not limit shunting; the direction and volume of shunt flow are governed by the pressure gradient created by the pulmonary stenosis.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Large non-restrictive VSD = allows free shunting (driven by pressure gradient, not VSD size)

wrongOptions.text: C) The extent of right ventricular hypertrophy
wrongOptions.explanation: RVH is a secondary consequence of chronic pressure overload from pulmonary stenosis, not the primary driver of cyanosis.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: RVH in TOF = secondary to pulmonary stenosis (consequence, not cause)

wrongOptions.text: D) The degree of aortic override
wrongOptions.explanation: The overriding aorta straddles the VSD and contributes to mixing, but variations in override are not the primary determinant of cyanosis severity.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Overriding aorta = anatomic feature of TOF (not the main severity driver)

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Severity of cyanosis in TOF = degree of pulmonary stenosis (RV outflow obstruction)

stem: A cyanotic child's chest radiograph demonstrates a boot-shaped cardiac silhouette. This finding is most consistent with:
explanation: The boot-shaped heart (coeur en sabot) is produced by right ventricular hypertrophy lifting the cardiac apex upward, combined with a concave pulmonary trunk from pulmonary stenosis. It is the classic chest radiograph finding of Tetralogy of Fallot.
topicName: Tetralogy of Fallot — boot-shaped heart on CXR

wrongOptions.text: B) Transposition of the great arteries
wrongOptions.explanation: TGA produces an "egg-on-a-string" silhouette from a narrow mediastinum and globular heart.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Egg-on-a-string CXR + newborn cyanosis = TGA

wrongOptions.text: C) Total anomalous pulmonary venous return
wrongOptions.explanation: TAPVR (supracardiac type) produces a "snowman" silhouette from dilated vertical vein and SVC.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Snowman CXR + infant cyanosis = TAPVR

wrongOptions.explanation: Tricuspid atresia shows a small RV and left-axis deviation on ECG, without a characteristic boot-shaped silhouette.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Left-axis deviation + cyanotic infant + small RV = tricuspid atresia

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Boot-shaped heart + cyanotic child = Tetralogy of Fallot
tags: Tetralogy of Fallot — boot-shaped heart on CXR

stem: A 61-year-old man presents 15 months after his wife's death. He continues to experience daily intense yearning for her, believes his life has no purpose without her, avoids all places associated with her, and has been unable to return to his volunteer work. He denies depressed mood outside the context of missing her and continues to find pleasure in watching his grandchildren. The feature most specific to prolonged grief disorder (rather than MDD) in this presentation is:
explanation: Prolonged grief disorder is characterized by grief-specific symptoms: persistent yearning/longing for the deceased, identity disruption (loss of sense of self without the deceased), difficulty accepting the death, and bitterness,  all anchored specifically to the loss. Critically, the capacity for non-grief-related pleasure is preserved (he still enjoys grandchildren), which distinguishes PGD from MDD. In MDD, anhedonia is pervasive and not restricted to grief content. The combination of grief-specific distress + preserved pleasure capacity outside grief context = PGD, not MDD.
topicName: Prolonged Grief Disorder — Distinguishing Features from Normal Grief and MDD

choices.text: Persistent yearning and longing for the deceased with grief-anchored identity disruption, in the presence of preserved capacity for non-grief-related pleasure
Weight loss and insomnia occurring in the context of a major loss
Passive wish to die in order to be reunited with the deceased
Duration of symptoms exceeding 2 weeks with functional impairment

wrongOptions.text: 1: B) Weight loss and insomnia in context of loss
wrongOptions.explanation: Weight loss and insomnia are neurovegetative symptoms that occur in both normal grief, PGD, and MDD. They do not distinguish PGD from MDD. The distinguishing feature is the grief-specificity of symptoms and the preservation of non-grief-related pleasure.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Neurovegetative symptoms (insomnia, weight loss) = present in grief AND MDD, non-specific for PGD diagnosis

wrongOptions.text: 2: C) Passive wish to die to be reunited with the deceased
wrongOptions.explanation: A passive death wish to be reunited with the deceased ('I want to join him') is a grief-specific phenomenon common in both normal grief and PGD. It is not suicidal ideation in the MDD sense (which involves escape from worthlessness or hopelessness), and while it supports PGD, it is not the most specific distinguishing feature from MDD. The preserved pleasure capacity is a more specific differentiator.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Passive death wish ('want to join deceased') = grief-specific but not the single most distinguishing feature from MDD

wrongOptions.text: 3: D) Duration exceeding 2 weeks with functional impairment
wrongOptions.explanation: The 2-week minimum duration with functional impairment is the diagnostic threshold for MDD, not PGD. PGD requires a minimum of 12 months duration (DSM-5-TR). Two-week duration would not meet PGD criteria at all.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: ≥5/9 symptoms for ≥2 weeks with impairment = MDD duration threshold; PGD requires ≥12 months

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Yearning + identity disruption + functional impairment + preserved non-grief pleasure = Prolonged Grief Disorder (not MDD)
tags: Prolonged Grief Disorder — Distinguishing Features from Normal Grief and MDD

stem: A 34-year-old man with intense unconscious rage toward his abusive father channels this energy into becoming a highly decorated emergency medicine physician who is known among colleagues for his exceptional care of trauma patients. He has no conscious awareness of the connection between his unresolved anger and his professional identity. The defense mechanism he is utilizing is:
explanation: Sublimation is a mature defense mechanism in which energy from unacceptable unconscious impulses (rage, aggression, sexual drives) is redirected into socially acceptable, constructive, and often professionally productive behaviors. It is considered the most adaptive defense mechanism because the underlying drive is not suppressed or denied,  it is transformed. The key features in this vignette: (1) unconscious rage (not consciously acknowledged); (2) the energy is channeled into a socially valued activity (medicine, specifically trauma care,  which involves managing the consequences of physical harm); (3) the patient has no conscious awareness of the connection. Sublimation is distinct from reaction formation (behaving the opposite of the impulse) because the energy is channeled, not inverted.
topicName: Defense Mechanisms — Sublimation (Mature) vs Reaction Formation vs Displacement

choices.text: Sublimation — redirecting socially unacceptable impulses into socially valued and constructive activities
Reaction formation — behaving in a manner diametrically opposite to unacceptable unconscious impulses
Displacement — redirecting an emotional response from its original target to a substitute, less threatening target
Rationalization — constructing a logical justification for behaviors driven by unconscious motives

wrongOptions.explanation: Reaction formation involves behaving in a manner directly opposite to an unacceptable unconscious impulse. A classic example: a person with unconscious homosexual impulses who becomes vocally homophobic; or a person who unconsciously dislikes a colleague but is excessively and performatively kind to them. In this vignette, the physician is not inverting his rage (becoming pacifist, anti-violence, or excessively gentle as a direct contradiction) — he is productively channeling it. Channeling ≠ inverting.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Unconscious impulse → opposite behavior on the surface (excessively kind when unconsciously hostile) = Reaction formation

wrongOptions.explanation: Displacement redirects an emotion from its original, threatening target to a safer substitute target. Example: a person who is furious at their boss but comes home and yells at their spouse. In displacement, the emotion remains the same (anger) but is aimed at a different, less threatening object. In this vignette, the physician is not redirecting anger onto a substitute target,  he is transforming the energy into a productive career, which is sublimation.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Anger at boss → yells at spouse; fear of parent → aggressive toward pet = Displacement (same emotion, different target)

wrongOptions.explanation: Rationalization involves providing a logical, consciously acceptable explanation for a behavior that is actually driven by unconscious motives. The physician in this vignette has no conscious explanation or justification for the connection between his rage and his career,  he has no awareness of it at all. Rationalization requires the person to offer (a false) reason. Sublimation operates entirely outside conscious awareness.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: I was just being efficient, not rude' = Rationalization (post-hoc logical justification for unconsciously motivated behavior)

buzzwords: channels energy into socially constructive activity
buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Unconscious impulse → channeled into socially productive activity + no conscious awareness = Sublimation (mature defense)
tags: Defense Mechanisms — Sublimation (Mature) vs Reaction Formation vs Displacement
channels energy into socially constructive activity

stem: A 17-year-old girl is diagnosed with gonorrhea and asks her physician not to tell her parents. She is not in danger and denies abuse. Which of the following is the most appropriate physician response?
explanation: Adolescents can generally consent to confidential diagnosis and treatment of sexually transmitted infections. Disclosure without consent is unnecessary unless there is concern for abuse or danger.
system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills

choices.text: “I am legally required to inform your parents because you are a minor.”
“I can only provide treatment if your parents consent.”
“You should return with a parent before I prescribe antibiotics.”

wrongOptions.text: A) “I am legally required to inform your parents because you are a minor.”
wrongOptions.explanation: Routine STI diagnoses in adolescents do not require automatic parental notification.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Minor status + STI + Mandatory disclosure misconception = Incorrect parental notification

wrongOptions.text: C) “I can only provide treatment if your parents consent.”
wrongOptions.explanation: Parental consent is not generally required for STI treatment in minors.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Adolescent STI + Need for antibiotics + False consent requirement = Incorrect delay in care

wrongOptions.text: D) “You should return with a parent before I prescribe antibiotics.”
wrongOptions.explanation: Delaying treatment until parental involvement may discourage adolescents from seeking care.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Confidential request + STI symptoms + Delayed treatment = Ethical violation

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Minor patient + STI diagnosis + No safety concern = Maintain confidentiality
tags: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills

stem: A 15-year-old boy requests contraception counseling and asks that the discussion remain private from his parents. Which of the following is the best physician response?
explanation: Confidential reproductive health counseling encourages adolescents to seek appropriate medical care and is generally protected unless safety concerns are present.
system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
correctAnswerText: B) “I will keep this discussion confidential.”

choices.text: “I must obtain parental permission before discussing contraception.”
“Your parents are entitled to know about all reproductive health visits.”
“Confidential counseling is only available after age 18.”

wrongOptions.text: A) “I must obtain parental permission before discussing contraception.”
wrongOptions.explanation: Parental permission is not generally required for confidential contraceptive counseling in adolescents.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Teenager + Contraception request + False parental requirement = Incorrect restriction

wrongOptions.text: C) “Your parents are entitled to know about all reproductive health visits.”
wrongOptions.explanation: Confidential reproductive healthcare is commonly protected for adolescent patients.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Minor patient + Confidential counseling + Automatic disclosure misconception = Ethical breach

wrongOptions.text: D) “Confidential counseling is only available after age 18.”
wrongOptions.explanation: Adolescents may receive confidential reproductive counseling before adulthood.
wrongOptions.buzzwordCombo: Age under 18 + Reproductive counseling + Denial of confidentiality = Incorrect practice

buzzwordCombinationCorrect: Minor patient + Reproductive counseling + No safety concern = Confidential care
